title: The mechanism of 5 and 6 August 2019: who supplied the concurrence, and who supplied the recommendation
summary: Article 370 was rendered inoperative by two Presidential orders four days apart. C.O. 272 of 5 August 2019 superseded the Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order 1954, applied the whole Constitution to the State, and added a clause to Article 367 directing that the expression 'Constituent Assembly of the State referred to in clause (2)' in the proviso to Article 370(3) be read as 'Legislative Assembly of the State'. C.O. 273 of 6 August 2019 then declared, on the recommendation of Parliament, that all clauses of Article 370 cease to be operative. A five-judge Constitution Bench held on 11 December 2023 that the Article 367 route was ultra vires and that the identical result was independently available without it, and disposed of every petition.
claimAtLaunch: The Ministry of Home Affairs release of 6 August 2019 is headed 'Parliament approves Resolution to repeal Article 370; paves way to truly integrate J&K with Indian Union'.
whatHappened: The chain runs through eight dated instruments, all four of the operative ones retrieved. 20 June 2018: Governor's Proclamation under section 92 of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir. 21 November 2018: the Governor dissolves the Legislative Assembly under section 53(2) of that Constitution. 19 December 2018: President's Proclamation under Article 356, by which the functions of the State Government and the powers of the Governor are assumed by the President and the powers of the State Legislature become exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament. 5 August 2019: C.O. 272, whose own preamble recites that the President acts 'with the concurrence of the Government of State of Jammu and Kashmir'. 6 August 2019: C.O. 273, reciting the recommendation of Parliament. 9 August 2019: assent to the Reorganisation Act and notification S.O. 2889(E) appointing 31 October 2019. The Supreme Court found the concurrence question as a fact at paragraph 421 - 'However, it was the President giving concurrence' - and stated at paragraph 426 that the purpose of the concurrence condition 'would be lost if the President secures his own concurrence while exercising the power'. It then held at conclusion 514(h) that no concurrence of the State was required in the first place, which makes the recital in C.O. 272's own preamble surplusage. Conclusion 514(g) holds paragraph 2 of C.O. 272 ultra vires Article 370(1)(d) because an interpretation clause cannot be used to bypass the procedure for amendment; Khanna J's formulation is that it is 'ultra vires and bad in law, albeit can be sustained in view of the corresponding power under Article 370(1)(d)'. Two of the three opinions differ on the premise: Kaul J holds that J&K retained an element of internal sovereignty which Article 370(3) de-recognised, the majority holds it retained none after 1949, and Khanna J describes the two as uniform and concurs with both. The ratio on the sovereignty question is therefore not single.
caseFor: Article 370 sat in Part XXI of the Constitution under the heading 'Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions', and a unanimous Constitution Bench held it temporary on exactly that ground - 'the historical context for the inclusion of Article 370 and the placement of Article 370 in Part XXI'. Its own clause (3) vested an unqualified power in the President to declare it inoperative; the Court held that power did not lapse when the Constituent Assembly dissolved in 1957, because only the transitional recommending power in the proviso ceased, and that the President 'can unilaterally issue a notification that Article 370 ceases to exist'. The process was not executive fiat: both Houses passed resolutions recommending the declaration and both passed the Reorganisation Bill, and Article 3's first proviso requires only the State legislature's views, which the Court held are recommendatory as a matter of general constitutional law and not as a concession made for this case. Every substantive challenge was examined and rejected - sovereignty, the two Proclamations, the scope of Article 356, the application of the whole Constitution, and C.O. 273 itself. Where a defect was found, in the Article 367 route, the Court held the identical result independently available under Article 370(1)(d) and 370(3), so nothing turned on it. Not one petition was allowed.
caseAgainst: The concurrence of the State was given by the Union to itself, and the Supreme Court found this as a fact rather than as an allegation: 'However, it was the President giving concurrence since the Governor had by then dissolved the Legislative Assembly of State and the President by the 2018 Proclamation assumed to himself all the functions of the Government of the said State'. The same judgment states the objection to that in the Court's own words - the purpose of collaboration and representative democracy 'would be lost if the President secures his own concurrence'. The recommendation travelled the same route: the proviso to Article 370(3) required the Constituent Assembly's recommendation, C.O. 272 changed that to the Legislative Assembly, the Legislative Assembly had been dissolved by a Union-appointed Governor eight months earlier, its powers had been vested in Parliament by the President, and C.O. 273 recites Parliament's recommendation. At no point in the chain did any body chosen by the electorate of Jammu and Kashmir act. The Court held the device that made this possible ultra vires, in terms that concede the objection - 'the Legislative Assembly cannot be equated to the Constituent Assembly'; 'An interpretation clause cannot be used to bypass the procedure laid down for amendment' - and then held the vice immaterial because the same end was reachable by a route that dispenses with consent altogether. The one question that would have tested the outcome rather than the route, whether a State may be converted into a Union Territory, was framed for determination and then not determined, on the strength of counsel's statement that statehood would be restored.
differentFactsNote: The case for counts instruments and outcomes - 106 Central Acts applied by the Fifth Schedule, the whole Constitution applied by C.O. 272, a temporary provision ended by C.O. 273 and upheld by a unanimous Constitution Bench. The case against counts consents and adjudications - that the concurrence recited in C.O. 272 was given by the President to himself under a Proclamation that had vested the State's functions in him, a finding the Court itself made at paragraph 421; that the recommendation under Article 370(3) came from Parliament exercising the dissolved State legislature's powers; and that whether a State may be converted into a Union Territory is the one question the Court declined to decide. Both are arithmetically and legally correct, and granting either in full leaves the other intact. There is no measure of which a count of extended statutes and a declined constitutional question are both values, and the counterpart to the count is unadjudicated by the Court's own statement, so no common denominator could be constructed even in principle. One document holds both sets of facts - the judgment of 11 December 2023 contains the count, the holding, the finding of self-concurrence, the ultra vires holding and the declined question - but a common document is not a common ledger.
assessmentNote: Scored contested rather than worked or failed because the two sides do not disagree about a single retrieved fact. They disagree about what a constitutional process is for: the case for treats it instrumentally, so the question is whether the power existed and the outcome is lawful, and the case against treats it constitutively, so the question is who was entitled to decide. No assessment value in the enum expresses a disagreement about the criterion of success, and contested is the closest on its written text - the evidence supports more than one defensible reading and this record does not choose between them.

title: The Fifth Schedule sorted the J&K statute book by which direction an institution faces
summary: On the appointed day the Fifth Schedule of the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act 2019 disposed of the territory's statute book in four tables. It extended 106 Central Acts, kept 7 State laws with amendments, repealed 164 State and Governor's Acts, and left 166 in force. In the repealed table are the J&K Accountability Commission Act 2002, the J&K State Commission for Women Act 1999, the J&K Protection of Human Rights Act 1997 and the J&K State Vigilance Commission Act 2011; in the retained table are the J&K Public Safety Act 1978 and the J&K Panchayati Raj Act 1989.
whatHappened: Counted directly from the Gazette text, not from any secondary summary, with each table checked for a complete sequence from 1 to its maximum with no gaps and no duplicates. Table-1, 'Central laws made applicable', 106 entries. Table-2, 'State laws which shall be applicable with amendments', 7. Table-3, 'State laws including Governor's Acts which are repealed', two sub-lists of 153 State Acts and 11 Governor's Acts, 164 in all. Table-4, 'State Acts including Governor's Acts that shall remain in force', 166. State-law entries disposed of in total: 7 + 164 + 166 = 337, of which 48.7 per cent repealed, 49.3 per cent retained unamended and 2.1 per cent retained with amendment. Within Table-1, classified by what the amendments column actually directs, 15 entries read 'Extended as whole' and 91 direct the omission of a J&K-specific exclusion clause or proviso, overwhelmingly the words 'except the State of Jammu and Kashmir'; 15 + 91 = 106, with no entry outside those two classes. So for 91 of the 106, the instrument of extension is a deletion. The named entries: Table-3 entry 1, the Accountability Commission Act 2002; entry 23, the State Commission for Women Act 1999; entry 117, the J&K Protection of Human Rights Act 1997; entry 164, the State Vigilance Commission Act 2011. Table-4 entry 97, the Panchayati Raj Act 1989; entry 123, the Public Safety Act 1978. Table-1 entry 86 omits the proviso to section 1(2) of the central Protection of Human Rights Act, which the Gazette itself misdates as 1994. Section 100 of the Act does provide for the transfer of proceedings pending before any 'tribunal, authority or officer' to the corresponding body, but defines 'corresponding' as the body before which the proceeding 'would have laid if it had been instituted after the appointed day' - and where the same Act abolished the authority on that day, no such body exists, leaving only a discretionary fallback that no retrieved document shows was exercised.
caseFor: For 91 of the 106 Central Acts in Table-1 the operative words are the deletion of a clause reading 'except the State of Jammu and Kashmir' from a statute that already protected every other Indian. The Ministry of Home Affairs, answering the Rajya Sabha on 7 February 2024, named eight of them - the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009, the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition Act 2013, the Forest Rights Act 2006, the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989, the Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014, the Juvenile Justice Act 2015, the National Commission for Minorities Act 1992 and the National Commission for Safai Karmacharis Act 1993 - and said that residents of the region now enjoy rights available to citizens elsewhere. The repealed State commissions did not vanish into nothing: their central counterparts - the National Human Rights Commission, the National Commission for Women, the Central Vigilance Commission - were extended to the territory by the same schedule, and a national commission is not obviously a weaker forum than a State one. Retaining a preventive-detention statute and a panchayat statute in a territory with an active insurgency and a functioning local-government tier is an ordinary continuity decision, not a signal.
caseAgainst: The same schedule, on the same day, repealed the four State bodies to which a citizen of Jammu and Kashmir took a complaint against the state, and retained the statute under which the state takes a citizen's liberty without charge. The State Human Rights Commission was extinguished with roughly 630 complaints pending; the Accountability Commission, the Women's Commission and the State Vigilance Commission went with it. The Public Safety Act and the Panchayati Raj Act stayed. Nor is substitution by central bodies complete: section 19 of the central Protection of Human Rights Act leaves the National Human Rights Commission unable to investigate the armed forces, which is the class of respondent a J&K complaint is most likely to name, and Table-1 entry 86 omitted the proviso that had carved the erstwhile State out of that Act rather than the section that limits its reach. Section 100's transfer machinery, which Parliament did turn its mind to, cannot reach a proceeding whose forum the same Act abolished on the same day, and no document shows the discretionary fallback being used for a single one of the 630. The 337 entries also have no denominator: nothing states how many State enactments were in force on 30 October 2019, so the schedule cannot be read as a share.
differentFactsNote: Flagged false deliberately, because this is the judgement most at risk of being made silently. The two cases look as though they cross a category boundary - a count of laws extended against a claim about institutional design - but they do not, because both sides read the same instrument, and the instrument is a common ledger by construction. Table-1's 106 and Table-3's 164 and Table-4's 166 are columns of one schedule enacted on one day, and every entry either of the two sides relies on is in it. Granting the case for in full - that 91 exclusions were deleted and the central commissions extended - leaves entries 1, 23, 117 and 164 of Table-3 and entries 97 and 123 of Table-4 exactly where they are, and both sides can read them off the same page. This is a weighting dispute over one document, not a different-facts one.

title: The undertaking to restore statehood: seven years, six statements, no date
summary: The commitment to restore statehood to Jammu and Kashmir has been stated six times, in three forums, by the Union Home Minister, by two Ministers of State, by the Solicitor General and by the Supreme Court itself. It has never been withdrawn and has never been dated. As at August 2026 statehood has not been restored, and applications to enforce the undertaking are pending before the Supreme Court.
claimAtLaunch: Union Home Minister Amit Shah, replying to the Lok Sabha debate on 6 August 2019: 'I want to assure the people of J&K that the status of State would be restored once the situation normalises.'
whatHappened: The six statements, each with its forum and date. 6 August 2019, the Home Minister in the Lok Sabha, statehood restored 'once the situation normalises'. 20 November 2019, Rajya Sabha Unstarred Q.391, asking whether Government is prepared to give back statehood 'as early as possible' - the whole answer restates the Reorganisation Act in two sentences and does not address the question. 27 November 2019, Rajya Sabha Unstarred Q.1041, asked by Shri Nazir Ahmed Laway, seeking whether there is a proposal, 'if so, by when; and if not, the reasons therefor' - the same two sentences, and neither limb is answered. 15 December 2021, Rajya Sabha Unstarred Q.1959, asking for a timeline: 'Statehood to Jammu and Kashmir would be granted at an appropriate time.' 11 December 2023, the Solicitor General to the Constitution Bench, recorded by the Court: 'the statehood of Jammu and Kashmir will be restored (except for the carving out of the Union Territory of Ladakh)'. 11 December 2023, the Court at conclusion 514(n): 'Restoration of statehood shall take place at the earliest and as soon as possible' - no date, no addressee, no consequence, in the same sub-paragraph as a direction to the Election Commission that does carry a date. The two concurring formulations differ: the majority states elections and restoration as two obligations with no stated dependence between them, while Kaul J's conclusion (l) treats restoration as conditional on elections being held, which have been held since October 2024. A full-text sweep of 2,839 Ministry of Home Affairs parliamentary answers covering 152 sitting dates from January 2019 to July 2026 finds four mentioning statehood in any spelling: the three above, and one of 24 March 2026 that concerns Puducherry. In the Ministry's own published record of its own answers the subject has not been addressed in relation to Jammu and Kashmir since 15 December 2021. The Ministry's Annual Report 2024-25 contains zero occurrences of 'statehood' and zero of 'Article 370'.
caseFor: The undertaking has never been withdrawn, and the half of it that carried a date was performed: an assembly was elected in three phases in September and October 2024, counted on 8 October, and President's rule revoked by S.O. 4484(E) on 13 October 2024, putting an elected government in Srinagar for the first time in six years. Restoration of statehood is a legislative act requiring a Bill in Parliament, and the Government's position, stated to the Supreme Court in October 2025, is that it is in consultation with the territory and that security conditions including the Pahalgam attack of April 2025 warrant careful assessment - which is the same conditionality the Home Minister stated in 2019 and not a new one. The Court itself set no date and named no addressee, which is what a court does when it regards a matter as one for the political branch; Khanna J's own opinion says restoration is 'the prerogative of Parliament'. An undertaking framed as 'at the earliest and as soon as possible' cannot be said to have missed a deadline it never had.
caseAgainst: Seven years, four formulations, no date: 'once the situation normalises' (2019), 'at an appropriate time' (2021), 'will be restored' (2023), 'at the earliest and as soon as possible' (2023). None of the four is a testable condition, and none has ever been defined by anyone. The parliamentary route has been worked three times and produced two non-answers and one undated affirmation: a named member asked point-blank 'by when; and if not, the reasons therefor' on 27 November 2019 and was given a recitation of the Act that addressed neither limb. In the Ministry's own published record of 2,839 of its own answers, the subject has gone unmentioned for four and a half years, spanning the entire period since the Supreme Court said restoration shall take place at the earliest. The Ministry's flagship Annual Report for the year in which the territory got an elected legislature mentions neither the election, nor the judgment, nor the undertaking, nor Article 370. And the undertaking was load-bearing: it is the statement 'in view of' which the Court declined to decide whether a State may lawfully be converted into a Union Territory at all, so the one question that would have tested the conversion was set aside on the strength of a promise that remains unperformed.
assessmentNote: Filed too-early on the written definition - the measure is in force and has not run long enough for its stated objective to be testable - and the value strains, which is recorded here rather than resolved. The strain is that too-early was written for a measure that needs time to work, and this is an undertaking that needs a decision. Every alternative fails on its own text: no-objective fails because an objective was stated four times; contested fails because the evidence supports only one reading of whether restoration has occurred, and it has not; failed fails because no deadline was ever attached; reversed fails because the enacting authority has withdrawn nothing. This is the same shape as L-0086 - in force, testable in principle, awaiting external adjudication - and the two should be reviewed together. No new enum value is proposed. RESCORED too-early -> awaiting-adjudication on 2026-08-03, on the new value's written definition: in force, testable in principle, and the term that would settle it is a pending decision by a body outside the enacting authority. The value was added after a sweep of all 149 ledger records established the set was five, not the ten phase 11 estimated - and that only six records carried too-early at all, so 83 per cent of it held a state its definition did not describe. Four of the five take the new value; L-0139 does not, and is left as authored.

title: The election direction of 11 December 2023, and the dates the poll was actually completed on
summary: The Supreme Court directed that steps be taken by the Election Commission to conduct elections to the J&K Legislative Assembly by 30 September 2024. The Commission announced the schedule on 16 August 2024, polled the final phase on 1 October 2024, counted on 8 October 2024, and stated 10 October 2024 as the date before which the election should be completed. President's rule was revoked on 13 October 2024.
whatHappened: The direction, at conclusion 514(n) of the judgment: 'We direct that steps shall be taken by the Election Commission of India to conduct elections to the Legislative Assembly of Jammu and Kashmir constituted under Section 14 of the Reorganisation Act by 30 September 2024.' The dates, from two PIB reproductions of Election Commission material: schedule announced by Press Note ECI/PN/128/2024 on 16 August 2024; Phase-3 gazette notification 5 September 2024; counting originally 4 October and completion 6 October; final phase polled across 40 assembly constituencies on 1 October 2024; counting revised to 8 October 2024 for both J&K and Haryana; 'date before which election shall be completed' 10 October 2024. President's rule revoked by S.O. 4484(E) under section 73 of the Reorganisation Act on 13 October 2024. No document retrieved - not the Election Commission's releases, not the Ministry of Home Affairs Annual Reports, not any of 2,839 parliamentary answers - records the Government or the Commission addressing the 30 September date at all, in either direction.
caseFor: The direction's grammatical object is the taking of steps, not the completion of the poll: steps shall be taken to conduct elections by 30 September 2024. Steps were taken, publicly and on the record - the full schedule announced on 16 August, the Phase-3 gazette notification issued on 5 September, and two of three phases polled in September - so the election was in progress on the day named. The residual slippage is one polling day and a counting date, and the counting date moved for a reason recorded on the face of the Commission's own press note that has nothing to do with Jammu and Kashmir: the Haryana poll was rescheduled around a religious observance and the two counts were kept together. The elected Assembly was constituted and President's rule revoked within a fortnight of the date. On the Commission's own account the poll ran without a single repoll, with turnout above the 2024 Lok Sabha figure in the territory and with polling stations established in 469 locations along the Line of Control and the International Border.
caseAgainst: A judicial direction to conduct elections by a date is not discharged by having conducted some of them by that date. Five judges chose a specific date in a case about the removal of an elected legislature, and the date passed with the poll unfinished and no vote counted. The Commission's own original schedule, announced on 16 August 2024, already placed counting on 4 October - so the body under the direction planned from the outset to finish after the date, and no extension was sought or granted so far as any retrieved document shows. The Commission's own press material celebrating the poll does not mention the direction, the deadline, or the judgment at all. And no organ of the state has ever addressed the date: in 2,839 of the Ministry's own published parliamentary answers, in three Annual Reports and in the Commission's releases, there is neither a claim of compliance nor an explanation of the slippage.
differentFactsNote: Flagged false and noted, because the record looks superficially like a legal-ruling-against-a-quantity case and is not. Both sides accept every date in the sequence without qualification - 30 September as the direction, 16 August as the announcement, 1 October as the final poll, 8 October as the count, 10 October as the stated completion date, 13 October as the revocation. What divides them is what 'by' governs in the sentence the Court wrote, which is a reading of one document both sides hold. That is a weighting dispute over a shared ledger of six dates, not a different-facts one.
caveat: The election dates here are the Election Commission's own account of the Election Commission's own conduct, relayed under a government press-agency byline, at a moment when the Commission was under a judicial direction with a date attached. PIB is not a check on the Commission. The Commission's own site returned HTTP 403 and was not retrieved.

title: The official Constitution still prints the Article 367 substitution the Supreme Court held ultra vires
summary: The Legislative Department's pocket edition of the Constitution of India, dated 1 May 2024, prints the proviso to Article 370(3) as amended by C.O. 272 and footnotes the substitution as good law, four and a half months after a five-judge bench unanimously held that paragraph of C.O. 272 ultra vires. The printed text is also corrupt: it reads 'the recommendation of the clause (2) of Legislative Assembly of the State', which is neither English nor what C.O. 272 directed.
whatHappened: Article 370(3)'s proviso appears at page 233 of the 1 May 2024 edition as: 'Provided that the recommendation of the [clause (2) of Legislative Assembly of the State] shall be necessary before the President issues such a notification', with the footnote 'Subs. by C.O. 272, dated the 5-8-2019, s.2. for "Constituent Assembly of the State referred to in clause (2)" (w.e.f. 5-8-2019)'. Conclusion 514(g) of the judgment of 11 December 2023 holds that 'Paragraph 2 of CO 272 by which Article 370 was amended through Article 367 is ultra vires Article 370(1)(d)', and both concurring opinions agree. Nothing in the article, its footnotes or the preface refers to the judgment. The substitution has also been misapplied: C.O. 272(4)(d) directed that the whole expression 'Constituent Assembly of the State referred to in clause (2)' be read as 'Legislative Assembly of the State', and the edition has replaced only the leading words, stranding 'clause (2) of' in front. The preface presents Appendices II and III as neutral - 'have been provided respectively in Appendix II and Appendix III for reference' - with no note that any part of Appendix II has been declared ultra vires. Separately, the two official reproductions of C.O. 272 differ: the Legislative Department's Appendix II reads 'acting on the advice of his Council of Ministers' where the Supreme Court's judgment reads 'acting on the aid and advice'.
caseFor: The Court held paragraph 2 ultra vires and in the same breath held that the President could have reached the identical result under Article 370(1)(d), and upheld C.O. 273 in full; Article 370 is inoperative on either route. The appendices are printed 'for reference' and the footnote records what the instrument did, which is a historical fact that a later judgment does not undo. A pocket edition is a reference compilation and not a judicial reporter, and it is not the Legislative Department's function to annotate constitutional articles with the litigation history of the orders that touched them. The garbled line is a typographical error in a footnote-driven substitution, of a kind found in consolidations generally, and it changes nothing about the article's operation, which is that Article 370 has ceased to be operative.
caseAgainst: A pocket edition of the Constitution issued by the Government of India is the document a citizen, a magistrate and a law student read, and it currently tells them that a proviso reads in a way five judges of the Supreme Court unanimously said it cannot. The edition postdates the judgment by four and a half months, so this is not a timing problem. And the garbling is evidence about how the entry was made: the substitution was applied mechanically and the result was never read back, because 'the recommendation of the clause (2) of Legislative Assembly of the State' is not a sentence anyone checked. The correction is not hard to find, is not disputed, was made by the highest court in the country, and has not been carried into the official text.
assessmentNote: Filed contested on the written definition - the evidence supports more than one defensible reading and this record does not choose between them: an appendix-for-reference-with-a-historical-footnote reading, and an official-text-misstates-the-law reading, both available on the same document. The value strains for the same reason L-0092's does: this is a presentational finding, in which nothing in the world changed and what changed is what an official document says about the world, and no assessment value names that shape. failed is wrong because nobody announced an objective for a pocket edition. The record is filed on the definition and the stretch is recorded here. No new enum value is proposed, and this should be reviewed together with L-0092.

title: The Public Safety Act as it stood after the 2012 amendment: one limb narrowed, the other quadrupled
summary: Act VII of 2012 amended the Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act 1978. It is universally described as narrowing the Act - it barred detention of persons under 18, required grounds in a language the detenu understands, and cut the first-instance period on the security-of-the-State limb from two years to six months. It also raised the maximum on the public-order limb from twelve weeks to twelve months. This is the stated starting condition against which every post-2014 detention record in this phase is read.
whatHappened: Established from the official consolidated text of the Act on India Code, retrieved as a PDF after the host was reached by forcing DNS resolution, and read directly. Section 18 now reads: 'three months in the first instance which may be extended up to twelve months' for persons acting prejudicially to the maintenance of public order; twelve months for persons indulging in the smuggling of timber; and 'six months in the first instance which may be extended up to two years' for persons acting prejudicially to the security of the territory. The footnotes attribute both changes to the same instrument: 'Substituted for the words "twelve weeks" by Act VII of 2012, s. 6' and 'Substituted for the words "two years" ibid.' So the amendment did two opposite things in one section, and the half that appears in the secondary literature is the one that narrows. The public-order limb is the limb used against protesters and stone-pelters. The Act's complete list of amending instruments is Act II of 1982, Act IV of 1985, Act II of 1988, Act XII of 1988, Act VIII of 2001, Act VIII of 2002, Act VII of 2012, S.O. 3912(E) of 30 September 2019 and S.O. 1229(E) of 31 March 2020; the string '2018' does not occur anywhere in the Act.

title: The Public Safety Act was retained on the appointed day, adapted by executive order, and its Advisory Board transferred to executive selection
summary: The Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act 1978 survived the reorganisation at Fifth Schedule Table-4 entry 123, in the table of State Acts that remain in force. It was then adapted from State to Union Territory by executive order S.O. 1229(E) of 31 March 2020 made under section 96 of the Reorganisation Act, which also omitted the proviso to section 10 barring the lodging of permanent residents outside the territory and replaced the Advisory Board appointment provision. Selection of the Board that reviews detention orders now sits with a committee of three executive officers chaired by the Chief Secretary.
whatHappened: The composition qualification for the Advisory Board is untouched - the Chairman is or has been a High Court judge - and what changed is who chooses the person. Under the 1978 text members were appointed by the Government 'in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court'. On 22 May 2018 the Jammu and Kashmir (Preventive Detention Laws) Order 2018 removed the requirement to consult the Chief Justice, a change recorded by OHCHR in July 2019. On 31 March 2020 S.O. 1229(E) entry 104 substituted a new section 14(3) under which the Chairman and Members are appointed by the Government on the recommendations of a Search-cum-Selection Committee of the Chief Secretary as Chairman, the Additional Secretary of the Home Department and the Administrative Secretary of the Law Department, with judicial consultation surviving only where a sitting judge is to be appointed. The Home Department is the parent department of the detaining authorities. The same order substituted 'the Union territory of Jammu and Kashmir' for 'the State' throughout, and replaced the Ranbir Penal Code and the Samvat 1989 Criminal Procedure Code references with their central equivalents. The administration told the High Court that the Act 'shall be deemed to have been passed by the Parliament under Article 22(7)' - a claim that the Fifth Schedule converted a 1978 State enactment into parliamentary legislation, which matters because Article 22(7) is the clause under which Parliament, and not a State legislature, may prescribe detention beyond three months without an Advisory Board opinion. In May 2026 the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh upheld the adaptation in Tanveer Ahmad Mir v. Union Territory of J&K, 2026:JKLHC-SR:1587, holding that it fell within the power Parliament itself delegated by section 96, and dismissed the petition. Three press accounts date that judgment to 15, 16 and 18 May 2026 and the judgment itself was not retrieved, so no date for it is asserted here.
caseFor: Parliament made a deliberate legislative choice about a territory for which it had just assumed direct responsibility, and preventive detention is not an aberration in Indian constitutional law: Article 22 of the Constitution itself contemplates detention without trial and prescribes the safeguards that attend it. The theatre in which the Act operates is not hypothetical - 2008, 2010 and above all 2016 are documented instances of mass mobilisation converting rapidly into lethal violence - and the state's answer to the charge that it detains people who have committed no offence is that this is the entire point of preventive detention: to act on the organiser before the mobilisation, because a criminal prosecution requires a completed offence and the alternative instrument once the mobilisation happens is the bullet. The 2020 appointment reform replaced an unstructured 'consultation' with a written search-and-selection procedure of the kind used across Indian statutory tribunals, making the process repeatable and recorded where it had been neither. And the adaptation was tested in court by a detenu and upheld, on the ground that the parent Act itself conferred the power: once Parliament delegates by section 96, action taken under it cannot be ultra vires.
caseAgainst: The same Fifth Schedule that kept this Act repealed the State Human Rights Commission, the Accountability Commission, the Vigilance Commission and the Women's Commission. The bodies that received a citizen's complaint against the state went; the statute by which the state takes a citizen's liberty without charge stayed. What the 2020 order then did to the Advisory Board is the sharper half: a tribunal whose function is to review the executive's own detention orders now has its members selected by a committee chaired by the head of that executive and seating the Home Department, which is the parent department of every detaining authority in the territory. The form of the body is judicial and the production of its membership is executive. The same order omitted the proviso that had confined detenus to prisons inside the territory, and did so by executive notification rather than by any legislature. And the constitutional footing the administration now asserts - that the Act is deemed to have been passed by Parliament under Article 22(7) - claims for a 1978 State enactment a status it did not have before 31 October 2019, on the strength of its inclusion in a schedule.
assessmentNote: Filed no-objective because no objective was stated at announcement against which any of these three acts could be scored. Neither the Fifth Schedule's retention of the Act, nor the Order of 22 May 2018, nor entry 104 of S.O. 1229(E) was accompanied by any statement of what it was meant to achieve, and none has a claim at launch anywhere in the retrieved record. The value asserts nothing about the quality of the finding: the mechanism is established from the official consolidated text and from the Gazette.

title: Two bodies review the same detention orders: one confirms almost all of them, the other strikes down four in five
summary: Detention orders under the J&K Public Safety Act are reviewed twice. The statutory Advisory Board, whose members the executive now selects, confirmed almost 99 per cent of the orders put to it. The High Court, on the same population of orders, quashed just over 81 per cent of those it examined - and on a private reading of its own docket, 161 of the 203 petitions from the 2019 cohort that reached a decision on the merits, which is 79.3 per cent. The gap between those verdicts, and the reason it does not change the practice, are the record.
whatHappened: The 99 and 81 per cent figures come from a Right to Information inquiry by Venkatesh Nayak of the Commonwealth Human Rights Initiative, published 2 August 2018 and covering 2016 to 2018, known here only through OHCHR's July 2019 update which reproduces it: 'while the PSA Advisory Board confirmed almost 99 percent of the detention orders, the Jammu and Kashmir High Court reversed over 81 percent of these detention orders.' The CHRI page returns HTTP 404 and was not retrieved. The docket reading is Rhythm Buaria's, from case-status entries on the High Court's website as at 18 January 2021, for petitions filed in 2019: 716 challenging PSA orders, 570 disposed, 161 quashed, 42 upheld, 232 declared infructuous, 146 pending. The rate depends entirely on the denominator and the three denominators tell three different stories - 161 of 716 filed is 22.5 per cent, 161 of 570 disposed is 28.2 per cent, and 161 of the 203 decided on the merits is 79.3 per cent. The 232 infructuous disposals are 40.7 per cent of all disposals: the detention ran its course before the court reached it. Mean time to a quashing at the Srinagar wing was 252.5 days against a first-instance public-order maximum of twelve months. The mechanism that reconciles a 79 per cent merits-quashing rate with an unchanged practice is in the statute: the proviso to section 19(2) directs that 'in computing the maximum period for which a person against whom such fresh order of detention has been issued may be detained, the period during which such person was under the earlier order of detention shall be excluded.' The clock restarts. Individuals have been held under up to eight successive orders and one man was booked for the thirty-seventh time. Section 22 bars any proceeding against an officer for anything done in good faith under the Act.
caseFor: Habeas corpus lies to the High Court and is used - hundreds of petitions a year - and the High Court quashes orders repeatedly, in reported judgments that name the responsible officers in blunt terms. A system in which a District Magistrate's order is struck down by a judge who compares it unfavourably with a traffic challan is a system in which judicial review is functioning, not one in which it has been suppressed. The Advisory Board operates within statutory time limits on every order, and its Chairman is or has been a High Court judge. The two bodies are also not doing the same job: the Board asks within weeks whether there is sufficient cause for detention on the material before it, while the Court asks months later whether the order as drawn survives legal scrutiny, and orders fail on the second test for reasons - non-application of mind, defective grounds, undisclosed material - that a body reviewing the substance in real time would not reach. The 99 and 81 per cent figures rest on a single RTI reply that no one in this phase has read, covering three years.
caseAgainst: Two bodies review the same orders and return near-opposite verdicts, and the one with the higher confirmation rate is the one the executive staffs. Where the Court reaches the merits it strikes down roughly four orders in five. In 40.7 per cent of disposals in the 2019 cohort it never reached the merits at all, because the detention had already expired: the remedy is not refused, it is outrun, and the mean 252 days to a quashing sits inside a twelve-month public-order maximum. And a quashing does not end the detention. Section 19(2) permits a fresh order where the earlier failed on a technical defect, and its proviso excludes the time already served from the new maximum, so the statutory ceiling constrains no individual's total detention at all. In 1999 the Home Department directed the Central Jail Srinagar in writing not to release quashed detenus without clearance from the Home Department and the CID; in September 2025 a man whose order had been quashed after more than 520 days remained in prison. A senior lawyer's account, recorded in 2011 and still descriptive in 2026, states the mechanism plainly: the authorities know the order will be quashed and know the process takes about six months, so the objective is achieved regardless, and they can keep doing it because no one holds them accountable. Section 22 is why that last clause is accurate rather than rhetorical.
differentFactsNote: Flagged false and noted, because the temptation is to mark it true and the reason it is false is the sharpest finding in the subject. The two cases look as though they cross a category boundary - a security justification against a legality verdict - but the High Court's habeas corpus docket is a single ledger on which a security-justified order and a legality verdict meet, order by order, and the 79.3 per cent merits rate and the 40.7 per cent infructuous rate are computed from that one dataset. A second common ledger exists and is T1: the 'Detained' prison series tabled in the Rajya Sabha on 4 December 2019 carries the mass-mobilisation spike the case for rests on, at 395 in 2016, and the persistence of elevated numbers through 2017 to 2019 that the case against rests on, in the same column of the same table. Criterion (c) says in terms that an unbuilt comparison fails it: the docket comparison has been built four times by private parties from public data and never once by the holder, and that is a gap in the instrument rather than a property of the argument.
caveat: The 99 per cent and 81 per cent figures rest on a Commonwealth Human Rights Initiative RTI reply that nobody in this phase has read, relayed through OHCHR. The quashing rates rest on a practising lawyer's reading of case-status entries on a court website, not on any court publication.

title: The August 2019 detentions: ten official figures, five objects, and the one question that was never answered
summary: Between November 2019 and March 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs gave Parliament ten different detention figures for Jammu and Kashmir - 5,161, 6,605, 7,357, 451, 396, 444, 389, 437, 613 and 627 - on at least five different objects, none of which any answer defines. On 11 March 2020 it stated the legal basis in terms, which settles the definitional question almost nobody has noticed was settled. It was asked at least eight times, once by the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, for the number of political leaders detained, and never gave one.
whatHappened: The sentence that settles it, from Rajya Sabha Unstarred Q.1958 of 11 March 2020: 'cumulatively 7357 persons including stone pelters, miscreants, over ground workers (OGWs), separatists, etc. were taken into preventive custody since August, 2019. Out of these, 451 such persons are presently under preventive detention, which includes 396 persons under Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act (PSA). Detentions have been made u/s 107 Cr.PC, as also under J&K Public Safety Act, 1978.' So the large circulating figures are preventive custody by executive magistrates under section 107 of the Criminal Procedure Code, with PSA detentions a subset: 7,357 is a CrPC-class number, 396 is the PSA number, and the government stated both. The only order count MHA has ever produced is from Rajya Sabha Unstarred Q.349 of 5 February 2020: 'detention orders were issued against 444 persons under the Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act (PSA), 1978, since August 2019. At present, 389 persons are in detention under PSA' - and note that even the order count is expressed per person, so the re-detention multiplier is invisible in it. The three largest figures are one running count with two silent scope changes: 5,161 on 20 November 2019 is stated as 'in Kashmir Valley'; 6,605 on 5 February 2020 answers a question headed 'DETENTIONS IN JAMMU, KASHMIR AND LADAKH'; 7,357 on 11 March 2020 states no geography at all. The start date moved too - 4 August in November 2019, 'August 2019' a week later, '1 August 2019' in the 2021 replies. On 5 February 2020 the same Minister gave two different 'still detained' figures on the same day, 389 and 437, because they count different populations. Across 1,301 replies grep-searched over four sittings the phrase 'Public Safety Act' appears in exactly five, and in three of those five only in the question. At least eight questions asked for a count of political leaders detained, including Lok Sabha Unstarred Q.1405 answered 20 September 2020 in the name of Shri Rahul Gandhi seeking 'the details of political leaders detained under the Public Safety Act in Jammu and Kashmir since August 5, 2019 and the period of detention'; every one was answered with the aggregate preventive-custody figure or with a statement that no person is under house arrest. The only leader-adjacent number ever given is 'Nil', for political leaders detained under the National Security Act, a statute nobody had alleged was in use. The first official total of any kind is the 5,161 tabled on 20 November 2019, roughly fifteen weeks after 5 August; no detention total from any J&K press briefing in August or September 2019 could be established.
caseFor: The figures were produced whenever Parliament asked. The Ministry told the Rajya Sabha on 5 February 2020 that detention orders had issued against 444 persons under the PSA and 389 were then in PSA detention; on 11 March 2020 that 451 were in preventive detention of whom 396 were under the PSA; and in the same answer it stated the legal basis in terms. On 4 December 2019 it tabled a six-year prison table showing detenu numbers and out-of-territory lodging year by year. The charge that the government concealed how many of the post-August-2019 detentions were under the PSA is not sustainable on the record: it was asked and it answered, and the answer was 396 of 451. That the figure has been widely ignored in favour of the 7,357 preventive-custody aggregate is a failure of the people quoting it. Nothing in 1,301 replies searched across four sittings shows the Ministry refusing to state a PSA number or claiming the data is not maintained, and the Entry-4 State-subject deflection it uses on prisons generally was not used on J&K detention questions. The apparent multiplicity of figures is what happens when different members ask different questions about different populations on different dates, and every one of the ten is internally consistent with its own question.
caseAgainst: Ten figures, five objects, and not one answer that says which. In a population where a single person can generate up to eight successive detention orders, and one man was booked for the thirty-seventh time, the difference between persons detained and orders issued is not a rounding matter, and no instrument declares which it counts. The three largest figures are one running count whose geography moves from the Kashmir Valley to Jammu-Kashmir-and-Ladakh to unstated inside sixteen weeks, with no note anywhere; a denominator that moves is not a series. For fifteen weeks after 5 August 2019 the government gave no total of any kind, while the only people in a position to count independently were under a communications blackout, which is why nothing from that window can be reconciled. When Parliament asked eight times how many political leaders had been detained - once in the name of the Leader of the Opposition, expressly under the PSA and expressly with periods - it was told eight times how many people in total were in preventive custody. The party-wise breakdown existed: a newspaper obtained a classification of 177 detained politicians by party from documents sourced in the security establishment, so somebody made that classification and it was not the newspaper. And the flagship instrument is silent - the Ministry's Annual Report for 2019-20, the year of the lockdown, contains zero occurrences of 'Public Safety Act' and zero of 'detenu'.
assessmentNote: Filed no-objective because no objective was stated at announcement against which any of these figures could be scored. No detention target, threshold or purpose was ever published, and the disclosures were made in answer to questions rather than as a claim. The finding - that ten figures on five undeclared objects were produced by one ministry over sixteen months - is firmly established on retrieved primaries and the value asserts nothing about its quality.
differentFactsNote: Flagged false, and the reasoning is worth stating because the tempting answer is true. The two sides do genuinely count different things, so criterion (a) is satisfied, and neither contradicts the other's arithmetic, so (b) is satisfied. Criterion (c) is not. Each of the three objects - a stock of detenus on a date, a flow of persons detained over a period, a flow of orders issued - is perfectly definable, and the state holds every one of them: every detention order carries a district-year serial number, so each District Magistrate necessarily knows how many were issued; the J&K Home Department produced a five-year year-wise transfer series on a single sheet in 2023; and the Ministry itself decomposed 451 into 396 PSA and 55 CrPC in one sentence, which is the reconciliation being asked for, done once. What is absent is not a measure that could not exist but a declaration of which measure each figure is, which makes this an unbuilt reconciliation - and an unbuilt comparison fails (c) expressly.

title: The power to hold a J&K detenu anywhere in India, and the information barrier it creates
summary: A proviso inserted in 2002 barred the lodging of J&K permanent residents in prisons outside the State. It was omitted by executive order on 31 March 2020, on the official consolidated text of the Act. At least 1,122 PSA detenus were moved out of the territory between 2018 and 2023, 408 were held outside at August 2023, and a prison in Uttar Pradesh has refused under the Right to Information Act to disclose even the number of J&K detenus it holds. A challenge to the power has been pending before the High Court since the Supreme Court transferred it on 16 May 2023.
whatHappened: The dating of the removal was in dispute across four accounts and is now settled on the official text, with one question left open. India Code's consolidated Act carries two footnotes to section 10: 'Words "in the State" omitted by Act VIII of 2002, s. 2' and 'Proviso omitted by S.O. 1229(E) dated 31.03.2020'. The Act's complete list of amending instruments contains no 2018 enactment and the string '2018' does not occur anywhere in it. OHCHR's July 2019 update nonetheless names a 'Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act (Amendment) Act, 2018, 13 July 2018' and records that at least 40 people, chiefly separatist political leaders, were transferred out following it. What the 2018 Act did, and why it left no trace in the consolidation, is not established. The consequence is that the 295 detenus the J&K Home Department records transferring out during 2019, and the 188 out-of-State detenus NCRB records in Uttar Pradesh at 31 December 2019, were moved while the proviso barring exactly that was, on the face of the official text, still in force. The transfer series itself is the only clean year-wise run in the subject: 44, 295, a stated zero, 146, 585 and 52 to 1 August 2023, totalling 1,122, with 408 held outside at that date. It is corroborated independently from the receiving end by NCRB's own Table 2.12B, which shows Uttar Pradesh holding zero out-of-State detenus at 31 December 2018 and 188 a year later - a fourth instrument, official, that agrees. The information consequence is documented: an RTI application received by Agra Central Prison on 29 August 2019 seeking the list of J&K detainees was refused, and the bare number was refused with it, on a 2008 circular of the Uttar Pradesh Administrative Reforms Department and a characterisation of the information as third-party data. Moving a detenu across the territorial boundary moved the RTI addressee with him, to a body with no relationship to the detenu's family, community, courts or press. One detenu died in Naini jail, Prayagraj, on 23 December 2019 and his family was informed only after his death.
caseFor: The administration's stated grounds are overcrowding, security within the correctional system, and avoiding the mingling of hardcore insurgents with other prisoners, with the 2018 escape of a militant from a Srinagar hospital cited as precedent - and a prison system in a territory with an active insurgency has a real interest in where it holds people it regards as organisers. Inter-State lodging of prisoners is not peculiar to Jammu and Kashmir: NCRB records 7,076 convicts held outside their own State at the end of 2021, with Haryana holding the largest share. The transfer figures are also not concealed: the J&K Home Department produced a five-year year-wise series of them on a single sheet, and the Ministry of Home Affairs tabled the State-by-State lodging in Parliament in December 2019. And the legality of the power is being tested by the ordinary route - a writ petition by the High Court Bar Association, and a constitutional-validity challenge the Supreme Court transferred to the High Court on 16 May 2023 - which is what a system with a functioning judicial remedy looks like.
caseAgainst: Since the removal of the proviso a detenu can be held anywhere in India, and 1,122 were moved between 2018 and 2023, of whom 585 in 2022 alone. That puts them and their case files hundreds of miles from their families and their counsel, in prisons where the RTI Act - which is the citizen's instrument - has already been used to refuse even the aggregate number of J&K detenus held, as third-party information. The transfer also removes the person from the only count that would show him: Prison Statistics India attributes an inmate to the State that holds the body, has no interstate transfer table for detenus at all where it has one for convicts and one for undertrials, and publishes only an aggregate 'belongs to other State' column that never names the origin. So the practice makes the detenu harder to reach, harder to litigate for, and invisible in the J&K row of the only official series. The reasons for the amendment were never given: OHCHR recorded in July 2019 that the State was obliged under the J&K Right to Information Act 2009 to provide 'detailed reasons, facts and materials that form the basis of this amendment' and had provided none - and that Act was itself repealed 115 days later by the same Fifth Schedule. And the transfers at scale were made while the proviso forbidding them was still on the statute book, on the Government's own consolidated text.
assessmentNote: Filed too-early because the power is in force, has operated on 1,122 people, and its lawfulness is testable and before a court that has not ruled. The value strains: too-early is written for a measure that has not run long enough for its stated objective to be testable, and here the obstacle is a pending judgment rather than elapsed time. contested would be wrong - the evidence does not support two defensible readings of the legality question; one reading awaits confirmation by the only body entitled to give it. This is the same shape as L-0086 and as L-0127 and the three should be reviewed together. No new enum value is proposed. RESCORED too-early -> awaiting-adjudication on 2026-08-03, on the new value's written definition: in force, testable in principle, and the term that would settle it is a pending decision by a body outside the enacting authority. The value was added after a sweep of all 149 ledger records established the set was five, not the ten phase 11 estimated - and that only six records carried too-early at all, so 83 per cent of it held a state its definition did not describe. Four of the five take the new value; L-0139 does not, and is left as authored.
caveat: The 1,122 and 408 figures come from two press accounts three months apart that both reproduce a single J&K Home Department document of 31 August 2023. That is one source seen twice, not two sources, and neither outlet reports verifying the arithmetic.

title: Thirteen years of J&K detenu counts, one undifferentiated cell, and a fall that is partly a change of address
summary: Prison Statistics India carries a J&K detenu count for every year from 2009 to 2022 except 2012. It peaks at 546 in 2022 - not in 2016 and not in 2019 - and it cannot separate a Public Safety Act detenu from any other kind, because no volume from 2009 to 2022 disaggregates detenus by the law they are held under. It attributes a detenu to the State that holds him, has no interstate transfer table for detenus, and changed its territorial referent at the 2019-2020 volume boundary, fourteen months after the referent itself changed.
whatHappened: The series, read from Table 3.3 (Concluded) in the pre-2016 volumes and Table 2.1 (Concluded) from 2016: 182, 409, 239, no figure for 2012, 72, 35, 90, 432, 212, 283, 404, 228, 252, 546. Ten volumes were retrieved as PDFs from Internet Archive snapshots of NCRB's own files after the host failed DNS resolution and three more from the live host after the resolver was forced, and every all-India total was checked against the independent trend line printed natively in PSI 2021 Chart 2.12 for the six years that chart covers; all six match exactly. The 2012 volume could not be retrieved by any route: the table PDFs were never crawled and the full-volume path shows a 404, a 644-byte stub, and further 404s. Three structural facts govern any reading. First, no law-wise split exists: the only chapter that classifies inmates by the law they are held under is titled and scoped to convicts and undertrials, and NCRB names the PSA once, in a footnote to two tables, in an illustrative list ending 'etc.', with no figures. Second, the unit of account is the holding State, stated once in the whole volume - detenus and convicts belong to the State 'where they are incarcerated' - and Table 2.12B publishes an aggregate 'belongs to other State' column that never names the origin, while Table 7.5 has four release columns and no transfer column where the convict and undertrial tables have one. Third, the volume-wide State/UT list moves J&K from the STATES block at Sl. No. 10 to the UNION TERRITORIES block at Sl. No. 33 between the 2019 and 2020 volumes, with Ladakh appearing as Sl. No. 34; 'Ladakh' returns zero occurrences in every volume up to and including PSI 2019 and 178 in PSI 2020. PSI 2019's reference date of 31 December 2019 is sixty-one days after J&K ceased to be a State, and the volume reports a State of Jammu & Kashmir with Ladakh folded in and no footnote at the row. Ladakh reports zero detenus in every year since it was split out while reporting 20 to 30 other inmates, so the referent change is real and its arithmetic effect on this series is nil - which is why it must be declared rather than inferred from a movement in the numbers. And the series stops at 2022 because the publication stopped: NCRB's own index returns 'no record found' for 2023 and 2024.
caseFor: The instrument does what it says and says what it does. The category is defined in the Glossary, the definition is stable across at least 2013 to 2021, the reference date is printed on every table, the domicile split is published, and the national aggregate is complete - the 215 detenus that Uttar Pradesh and Haryana held from elsewhere at the end of 2019 are in the all-India total of 3,223, in the wrong rows rather than lost. A volume that publishes the domicile of detenus at all is publishing more than the transferring authority ever did, and it is NCRB's published table that makes the transfer practice visible from the receiving end and corroborates a J&K Home Department document to the unit. Prison statistics are compiled from returns furnished by the prison department that holds the body, which is the only department that can count it; asking NCRB to attribute an inmate to a detaining authority in another State would be asking a compiler to audit its own contributors.
caseAgainst: The series is presented as a J&K detenu count and is three things it does not say it is. It is all preventive-detention laws, so a reader cannot get a PSA figure from it in any year, ever. It is a 31 December stock, and J&K released 339 detenus during 2021 while holding 252 at year end, so the stock understates throughput by more than half. And it excludes the detenus the J&K authorities moved out of the territory, who leave the J&K row and enter the row of the State that holds them, uncounted as J&K's. The apparent collapse from 404 in 2019 to 228 in 2020 spans the largest detention wave in the territory's recent history, and the instrument offers no mechanism to distinguish release from transfer from COVID decongestion. Nowhere does NCRB state that the J&K row is incomplete. And the peak of the series is neither 2016 nor 2019 but 2022, at 546 - in a year in which the same table shows Haryana holding 235 detenus of whom three were Haryana-domiciled, and J&K's own Table 7.5 row records 706 releases against a year-end stock of 546 with 540 of them in an unexplained residual bucket.
assessmentNote: Filed no-objective because the record finds something real about an instrument and no objective was stated at announcement against which the instrument could be scored. NCRB announces no target for its detenu tables and makes no claim about what they measure beyond the Glossary definition, so there is nothing to score worked, partly or failed against. The value asserts nothing about the finding's quality: the eleven-year series and all three structural facts are established on ten retrieved official volumes.

title: The August 2019 communications blackout: four defensible durations, and orders the state refused to produce
summary: Mobile networks, internet and landline connectivity in the Kashmir Valley were all discontinued on 4 August 2019, the day before the constitutional orders. Restoration was staged over eighteen months and the duration therefore has at least four defensible values, from roughly 163 days to roughly 551, depending on which restoration is counted as the end. The orders that imposed the restriction were never published, and when the Supreme Court directed their production on 16 October 2019 the Union claimed privilege and then supplied only samples.
whatHappened: Every date below is from a retrieved primary document. 4 August 2019: 'mobile phone networks, internet services, landline connectivity were all discontinued in the valley'. 5 August 2019: District Magistrates imposed section 144 CrPC restrictions on movement and public gatherings; the Kashmir Times Srinagar edition could not be distributed that day and could not be published from 6 August. 16 October 2019: the Court records the Solicitor General's submission that mobile and landline had been partly relaxed, without dates. 10 January 2020: judgment. 14 January 2020: fixed line to institutions managing essential services, 2G postpaid in five Jammu districts. 24 January 2020: 2G restored in all districts, whitelisted sites only. 31 January, 7 February and 24 February 2020: the whitelist runs 329, then 481, then 1,674 sites. 4 March 2020: the whitelist is abolished. 15 April 2020: fixed line without speed restriction. 5 February 2021: the speed restriction revoked, on the advice of a Special Committee then in its sixth meeting. The four durations, each with both endpoints retrieved: total blackout to first fixed-line restoration, about 163 days; to any mobile internet in the Valley, about 173; to an open non-whitelisted internet, about 213; to unrestricted-speed mobile internet, about 551. The 551-day figure is the one in general circulation and requires the most care, because from March 2020 there was an open 2G internet on postpaid and verified prepaid connections and an unthrottled fixed line from April. The two counters that publish the figure differ by a day - 551 against 552 - on whether the start is 4 or 5 August and whether endpoints are inclusive. On the orders themselves: not one document in the J&K Home Department's numbered suspension-order series is dated 2019, the series begins in January 2020 after the judgment, and the Department was publishing other orders on the same website throughout 2019, so the mechanism existed and the communications orders were kept off it.
caseFor: A shutdown is a preventive instrument against rumour-driven mass mobilisation, and the theatre has a documented history of exactly that in 2008, 2010 and 2016. The Supreme Court, in the judgment most often cited against the state, accepted the premise in terms: modern terrorism relies heavily on the internet, which is used to raise money, recruit and spread propaganda, and which 'provides an easy inroad to young impressionable minds'. The period following August 2019 did not produce the mass-casualty street unrest of those earlier years. Restoration was not indefinite and was not a single switch: it was staged, documented, and each stage was tied to an assessment, and every one of the dates above sits on a published order that was retrieved for this record. Asked in May 2020 to lift the restriction outright, the Court declined and constituted a review body instead - which is not what a court that thought the restriction indefensible would have done. The state is under no obligation to publish operational security orders in real time while an operation is running, and from January 2020 the J&K Home Department has published its numbered suspension orders continuously, with publication written into the order's own distribution list alongside the press and the Gazette.
caseAgainst: The longest shutdown recorded anywhere, imposed on a population of more than twelve million, and the orders that imposed it were never published - so proportionality review was impossible by design rather than by oversight. That is not a characterisation but the record: when the Court directed production on 16 October 2019 the Union first claimed privilege, then dropped it and produced samples, and the Court held that difficulty 'is not a valid ground to refuse production of orders'. The published series begins after the judgment, and the Department's website was carrying its other orders throughout 2019, so the absence is not the absence of a mechanism. The deepest point is about knowledge rather than about rights: the blackout disabled the instruments that would have measured its own effects. Every tracker of Indian shutdowns is built, by its own written admission, from newspaper reports, and the newspapers could not publish - so the single most consequential shutdown in Indian history is recorded in the most-cited tracker as one row citing a news website, with no end date and a status of 'Active' seven years later. On the official side, the Ministry told the Lok Sabha in September 2020 that 2G was 'not an impediment' to health, education and justice in Jammu and Kashmir, and fourteen months later told a parliamentary committee that no impact assessment is available with it at all, and that neither it nor the telecommunications department has ever conducted any study linking shutdowns to the disorder they are imposed to prevent.
differentFactsNote: The security case rests on incident counts the UT administration produces and the Union relays, on the absence of the mass-casualty unrest of 2008, 2010 and 2016, and on the stagedness of restoration. The rights case rests on a duration, a population, and a stated absence - unpublished orders, and therefore no possible proportionality review. Both are arithmetically correct and neither contradicts the other: grant every incident figure the State placed before the Court and the rights case is untouched, because it is not a claim that violence rose; grant the 551 days and the unpublished orders and the security case is untouched, because it is not a claim that the orders were published. They cannot be netted, and not because the netting is merely unbuilt. It would require two terms that do not exist: the violence that would have occurred without the shutdown, which has no control territory and no counterfactual and which the Government has told a parliamentary committee it has never assessed; and the proportionality record, which is precisely what was not published and was refused when the Supreme Court asked for it. Building the common ledger would require the very thing whose absence is the rights case's central claim. That is the schema's own admitted case - a quantity against a stated absence, with the counterpart declared unmeasurable - and not the unbuilt-comparison case it excludes.
caveat: Confidence is not uniform across this record's span. For 4 August 2019 to roughly mid-January 2020 there is no measurement of the subject independent of either a government that did not publish its orders or a press that could not file. Everything from January 2020 is far better evidenced.
assessmentNote: Scored contested rather than partly or failed because the two sides rest on different facts, neither of which is in doubt, and no measure exists on which the record could choose between them. The schema's contested definition fits on its own text: the evidence supports more than one defensible reading and this record does not choose. The scoring is not against a launch claim - no objective was announced for the suspension - but against the Supreme Court's directions of 10 January 2020, which is the same construction L-0081 uses and declares.

The stated reason moved from privilege to administrative difficulty, and those are different claims about different facts; what is contested is not whether the orders existed - samples were produced - but whether difficulty justifies non-production, which the Court answered.

This is one of the few routes in the corpus that is enforceable rather than requestable, and unlike the all-India case it has a specific refusal behind it rather than a general non-practice.

unmeasured.why: No count exists at any level, official or unofficial. The trackers count internet shutdowns; nobody counts movement orders. The orders are issued by individual magistrates and there is no central register, so if a holder were compelled tomorrow no single body could produce the series. The August 2019 restriction had two legs - the communications cut and the movement restrictions imposed by District Magistrates on 5 August - and the corpus records only one of them. The judgment's direction to publish covers both.

unmeasured.why: The Suspension Rules cover telecom services, which include telephony, and a Valley-wide suspension of voice calling and SMS was ordered for Republic Day 2020 - sixteen days after the judgment - and confirmed by a published Home Department order that was retrieved and read. Every tracker of Indian shutdowns counts internet only. So a suspension of the oldest and most basic telecom service is counted nowhere, by anyone, official or unofficial, and the instruments that exist are defined so as to exclude it. This is not that nobody has published the count but that the quantity has never been gathered.

unmeasured.what: Any assessment of the effect of the suspension, or of whether suspension achieves what it is imposed for
unmeasured.why: Both responsible Union bodies told a parliamentary committee they hold none, and each named the other. The telecommunications department said it is not assessing whether the objectives have been achieved and that responsibility lies completely with the Ministry of Home Affairs or the State Government; the Committee recorded that no assessment is available with the Ministry of Home Affairs; and both told the Committee they have not conducted any study to establish the link between internet shutdown and communal riots. Neither has studied the rules adopted in other democracies. A measure defended by its effects has never had its effects measured, and the Government said so to Parliament.

title: The Review Committee for J&K: findings refused as exempt, ordered released, then said not to exist
summary: The Review Committee is the only safeguard the Suspension Rules provide against misuse of the power, and the Rules require it to record findings. Asked twice under the Right to Information Act for the findings on J&K suspension orders, the Home Department refused them as exempt without naming a clause, was twice directed to release them by its own First Appellate Authority, did not comply, and then said the information was not available in its records. The Review Committee orders that have since surfaced are bare confirmations containing no findings at all, and one of them confirms orders passed 178 days earlier.
whatHappened: The chain, from the applicant's own published account. June 2023: an RTI to the J&K Home Department for the number of suspension orders issued since 10 January 2020, whether a Review Committee had been constituted, and its findings; everything disclosed except the findings, refused as exempt under section 8 without specifying which clause; first appeal 29 July 2023; the First Appellate Authority ordered release on 17 August 2023, recording that the Supreme Court had made no direction permitting a Public Information Officer to withhold Review Committee orders. May 2024: application IFF/RTI/2024/112 of 15 May 2024, same subject; refused 6 June 2024 on the same unparticularised ground; first appeal 6 July 2024; the Appellate Authority again ordered release on 5 August 2024; the officer did not comply; a compliance letter of 15 October 2024 produced the reply of 29 October 2024 that the information is 'not available in the records' of the department. A further appeal on 30 November 2024 produced a direction limited to orders issued after 23 February 2024, and a second appeal was filed. Separately, two Review Committee orders were retrieved from archive captures of the department's own files and read: Government Order No. 2128-JK(GAD) of 23 December 2024 and No. 249-JK(GAD) of 18 February 2025. Three things follow from them. They are published by the General Administration Department and not the Home Department, and sit in a GAD file, which supplies a candidate innocent explanation for the Home officer's answer - though under section 6(3) of the Right to Information Act a public authority that does not hold information must transfer the application rather than reject it. Each states only that the action 'has been confirmed by the Review Committee', with no finding of any kind, where both the 2017 and 2024 Rules require the Committee to record its findings as to whether the order accords with the statute. And the timing does not meet the five-day rule on the face of the published record: the December 2024 order confirms orders of 27 and 28 June 2024, 178 and 179 days earlier, while the February 2025 order confirms an order twelve days earlier; neither gives a meeting date, so whether the Committee met in time is not determinable from the document that exists to record its work.
caseFor: A Review Committee for Jammu and Kashmir demonstrably exists, meets, and has its confirmations published - established here from primary documents rather than from any applicant's account. Its composition matches what the Rules prescribe and the distribution of its orders is consistent with that composition. The department's two answers are not necessarily inconsistent: the review record sits with the General Administration Department and the applications were addressed to the Home Department, so an officer answering that the material is not available in his department's records may be departmentally accurate. The improvement across the statutory changeover is real and visible - a 178-day lag on the June 2024 orders against a twelve-day lag on the February 2025 one. And the Supreme Court's own position, as reported, is that the Committee's deliberations need not be published; what must be published is the order passed in the review, and those orders are published.
caseAgainst: What is published is a bare confirmation with no findings and no reasons, when the rule that constitutes the Committee requires it to record its findings as to whether the direction accords with the statute. If the order passed in review must be published so that it can be reviewed, an order containing nothing but the word 'confirmed' defeats the purpose exactly. On the two documents that exist, either the review was months late or the record of a timely review was published months late, and the published document cannot distinguish them - which is itself the finding, since a document whose function is to evidence timeliness omits the only date that would. And the department's own answers cannot both be true: in June it withheld the findings as exempt under section 8, which asserts they exist and are held, and in October it said they were not available in the records, which asserts they are not. If the second answer is the true one, then the Review Committee findings for January 2020 to February 2024 do not exist, and the only statutory oversight mechanism was not producing the record the rule requires - which is a materially worse finding than non-disclosure. Neither reading can be eliminated on the evidence held.
assessmentNote: Filed contested on the written definition, and the two defensible readings are named rather than chosen: either the findings exist and were withheld, or they do not exist and the safeguard was not operating. The distinction matters and cannot be resolved from the documents retrieved, and this record does not choose between them.
caveat: The RTI chain is known only through the applicant organisation's own published posts. The applicant is a party and not an observer, no appellate order was retrieved, and no J&K host was reachable to check any of it against the department's own records.
