title: The Union keeps no count of shutdowns because police is a State subject, and in Jammu and Kashmir it is not
summary: Both Union bodies with responsibility for telecom suspension have stated on the record that they keep no record of shutdown orders issued by States and Union Territories, and the reason both give is that police and public order are State subjects. Jammu and Kashmir is not a State: the Reorganisation Act places Public Order and Police outside the Legislative Assembly's competence entirely, and everything outside that competence is the Lieutenant Governor's discretion, on which no court may inquire what advice was tendered. So for the territory where suspensions have been most frequent and most prolonged, the constitutional ground the Union gives for not counting does not apply to it.
whatHappened: The Union's position, in its own words and from two retrieved primaries. On 10 March 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs told the Rajya Sabha: 'Centralized data of internet shutdown is not maintained by the Ministry of Home affairs. Orders issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) are available at MHA website.' In December 2021 a Lok Sabha standing committee printed the same position from both ministries: records of shutdowns ordered by State Governments 'are not maintained by Ministry of Home Affairs'; they 'are not maintained by DoT'; 'DoT does not maintain any information on State subjects'; and the Secretary in oral evidence, 'As Central Government, we do not have a mechanism in which we review as to how many States have given such orders ... essentially Police and Public Order are State Subjects.' The mechanism of the absence is stated by the Ministry itself: a functioning national counting apparatus exists, and internet suspension was defined outside it - 'the suspension of internet for purposes of public order, etc. does not actually come under the ambit of crimes. So, this is not within the present purview of the NCRB. At the moment, there is no proposal in MHA at least to collect this information at a central level.' The Committee's own conclusion was that consequently neither body is aware of the number of shutdowns imposed and there is no mechanism to verify any count. Against that, three retrieved sections of the Reorganisation Act: section 32(1) excludes Public Order and Police from the Legislative Assembly's competence; section 53(2)(i) makes any matter outside that competence one on which the Lieutenant Governor acts in his discretion, with his own decision on the scope of that discretion final; and section 53(3) bars any court from inquiring what advice Ministers tendered. A suspension is ordered on grounds of public emergency or public safety and, on the retrieved J&K orders themselves, in the interest of the security of the territory and for maintaining public order - squarely inside the excluded subjects. And in July 2022, asked in the Rajya Sabha whether it maintains data on the number of internet shutdowns in J&K and if not the reasons, the Ministry answered neither yes nor no, and told Parliament instead that the orders 'are uploaded on the official website of the Government of Jammu and Kashmir'.
caseFor: The constitutional argument is not a pretext in general: police and public order genuinely are State subjects, and a Union department declining to duplicate thirty-six States' and UTs' records is following the division of powers rather than evading scrutiny. The Union does publish its own orders and said so in the same breath as the disclaimer. Nothing in the Reorganisation Act obliges the Union to compile a statistical series, and record-keeping and aggregation are different questions: the orders are published individually and serially, so no information is being suppressed by the absence of a total. The Standing Committee's evidence was taken from the Department of Telecommunications about States generally, in a report about States generally, and the para-23 answer should not be read as a considered constitutional position about one Union Territory. The Union's answer of July 2022 also told Parliament exactly where the J&K orders are, which is more than a body concealing them would do.
caseAgainst: The Union's stated ground for holding no record is constitutional, and it does not fit the one territory where the power has been used most. Jammu and Kashmir is not a State; Public Order and Police are outside its Assembly's competence by statute, they run to the Lieutenant Governor as a matter of his discretion, and section 53(3) forecloses even judicial inquiry into what advice was tendered. So the accountability route that exists in every State - an elected Home Minister answerable to a State Assembly for a shutdown - does not exist in J&K at all, and the Union is the authority. That this is a legislative design choice rather than a seizure of power makes it a stronger fact, not a weaker one. And the record shows the Union knows perfectly well where the J&K orders are: it pointed Parliament to the website. The position that emerges from the two documents together is that the Union does not count J&K's suspensions, says it need not because police is a State subject, J&K is not a State, and the Union can nevertheless say precisely where the orders are published. That is not an inability to obtain the data. It is a declined aggregation, and the mechanism is stated by the Ministry itself: a national counting apparatus exists, the phenomenon was classified out of its scope, and there is no proposal to bring it in.
assessmentNote: Filed no-objective because no objective was ever stated at announcement against which the non-collection could be scored. Nobody announced a decision not to count shutdowns; the position emerges from answers given when asked, and the only stated purpose in the record is the Standing Committee's recommendation, which is a recommendation to the Government and not a claim by it. This follows the value's use on the phase-11 records that find a quantity has no instrument, which are decided the same way. ON THE STRENGTH OF THE CASES, RECORDED RATHER THAN REPAIRED: the caseFor here is thin, and it is thin because the position it has to defend is PROCEDURAL and, on this record's own facts, UNAVAILABLE. The Union's stated reason for not aggregating is that police and public order are State subjects. That reason is sound in general and cannot apply to Jammu and Kashmir, where the same Reorganisation Act this record cites removes Police and Public Order from the Legislative Assembly's competence by section 32(1) and routes them to the Lieutenant Governor and thence to the Ministry itself. So the strongest available case for is left arguing a constitutional division that the territory in question is the one exception to, and the record establishes that exception from the statute rather than by inference. THE CASE HAS NOT BEEN STRENGTHENED TO COMPENSATE. Padding it with a better argument than the government has actually made would be authoring a defence rather than reporting one, and a caseFor that is weak because the position is weak is a finding about the position, not a defect in the record. A reader should read the imbalance as evidence.

title: The 2024 Suspension Rules in J&K: narrow, timed and reason-bearing orders under an untested regime
summary: The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules 2024 commenced on 22 November 2024, writing publication of every suspension order, a fifteen-day ceiling, a least-intrusive-means test and a power to set orders aside into binding subordinate legislation. They are being applied in Jammu and Kashmir, and the resulting orders are narrower than anything the earlier regime produced: restricted by service class, by a stated radius around named coordinates, and to a window measured in hours - and they state a reason.
claimAtLaunch: The Rules' own face: every suspension order shall be published, a suspension shall not exceed fifteen days, the least intrusive means shall be used, and a review committee is empowered to set an order aside.
whatHappened: The statutory changeover is visible on the face of the J&K orders. Government Order No. Home-11 (TSTS) of 2024, dated 4 November 2024 - eighteen days before commencement - still cites the 2017 Rules. Government Order No. Home-01 (TSTS) of 2025, dated 14 January 2025, confirms a direction of the Inspector General of Police, Kashmir Zone as Authorized Officer 'under sub rule (1) of Rule 3 of Temporary Suspension of Telecommunication Service Rules, 2024' read with section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act 2023, suspending 3G, 4G and 5G mobile data and allowing only 2G at not more than 128 Kbps in the Gund and Kangan areas of District Ganderbal, within a 20 kilometre radius of a stated latitude and longitude, from 0600 to 1630 hours on 13 January 2025. The November 2024 order is narrower still: a polygon in District Kathua given as four corner coordinates, from 0930 to 1600 on a single day. Both state a reason on the face of the document - the possibility of misuse of high-speed data by anti-national elements to spread misinformation and inciting material, with reference to numerous prior occasions. Set against a Valley-wide cut of indefinite duration in August 2019, that is a different instrument used differently. What has not been established is whether the Rules are working: whether every J&K order issued after commencement is in fact published with reasons, and whether any order has ever been set aside by a review committee. The published Review Committee orders that exist contain no findings at all, and one drafted under the new regime names a rule-set that does not exist, conflating the 2017 Rules' short title with the new year.
caseFor: The Rules go further than the judgment required and put in binding subordinate legislation what previously depended on a direction: publication of every suspension order, a fifteen-day ceiling on any single order, a least-intrusive-means test, and a review committee empowered to set an order aside rather than merely to record findings. They are demonstrably in force and in use in Jammu and Kashmir, and the orders made under them are as narrow as the instrument allows - a service class rather than a blanket cut, a stated radius around named coordinates rather than a division or a territory, and a named window of hours rather than an indefinite period. And they state a reason on the face of the published document, which is precisely the thing that was absent in 2019. Whether the reason is sufficient for proportionality review is a separate question; that a stated reason exists on a published order is a fact.
caseAgainst: The Rules have not been tested and the instrument that would test them is missing. The review orders published under the new regime are bare confirmations containing no findings, where both the old and the new rule require the committee to record its findings, so the power to set an order aside has produced no reviewable record of having been considered. Rule 3(2) requires publication of any suspension order issued under sub-rule (1), and sub-rule (1) is the provision under which the Authorized Officer issues - but on every J&K order retrieved, the document that directs the service providers is the police order and the document published is the Home Department's confirmation of it. Whether that discharges the rule is unresolved. The proviso permitting issuance in unavoidable circumstances specifies an officer not below the rank of a Joint Secretary to the Central Government, and the retrieved orders show an Inspector General of Police issuing under it, with no authorisation instrument located under either regime. And the venue on which all of this compliance is published has since ceased to resolve.
assessmentNote: Filed too-early on the written definition without strain: the measure is in force, commenced 22 November 2024, and has not run long enough for its stated objective to be testable. The objective is stated on the Rules' own face, which is unusual in this phase, and the thing that would test it - whether every J&K order after commencement is published with reasons and whether any has been set aside - is not established. The tension worth recording is that too-early presumes time alone will settle the matter, and here what would settle it is an act of publication by a holder whose website no longer resolves and whose review findings were, five months apart, described by the same department as both exempt and non-existent. This is the L-0086 shape and should be reviewed with it. No new enum value is proposed. CONSIDERED FOR awaiting-adjudication ON 2026-08-03 AND DELIBERATELY NOT MOVED. The value was added in the same commit for the four records whose obstacle is a pending decision by a body outside the enacting authority. This record is the fifth member of the shape as the sweep drew it, and it is the one that contradicts the value's own definition: what it awaits is an ACT OF PUBLICATION BY A HOLDER - a year of post-commencement orders at a live address, or a review order carrying an actual finding - not a ruling by an adjudicator. Those accumulate with time, which is what too-early describes. Stretching the new value to absorb this record would have repeated the defect the whole exercise exists to undo: reversed came to cover two mechanisms because a value was widened to fit a member rather than a member filed on the value's text. The boundary is recorded here so the next reader can test it rather than rediscover it.

title: The venue where J&K published its suspension orders no longer exists, and the live copies are held by two private organisations
summary: Every J&K suspension order published between January 2020 and 2025 was posted on the Home Department's website. That domain returns NXDOMAIN from three independent public resolvers, with a sibling government host resolving normally through the same resolver as a control, and its last archive capture is 3 April 2025. It is the address the Union gave the Rajya Sabha in July 2022 as the place where J&K suspension orders are uploaded.
whatHappened: The name does not exist in DNS on 1.1.1.1, 9.9.9.9 or 208.67.222.222; a second public resolver returns SERVFAIL, consistent with a resolver artefact affecting that resolver generally rather than with the host. The control is decisive: a sibling government host on the same second-level domain resolves and returns HTTP 200 through the same resolver in the same command, so this is neither a delegation problem nor the resolver artefact that produced several false negatives elsewhere in this phase. The last successful capture of the site root is 3 April 2025 and there are none in the sixteen months since. What was on it: the whole numbered suspension-order series from January 2020, the restoration order of 5 February 2021, the two Republic Day confirmations of January 2020, the November 2024 and January 2025 orders under the new regime, and the two General Administration Department review confirmations. Every J&K government document used in this phase was retrieved from the Internet Archive or from a non-governmental server. A shutdown tracker maintained by a legal-services organisation re-hosts the 2025 J&K orders on its own infrastructure rather than hotlinking them, and holds at least eleven of them; one was retrieved live from that server, rendered, read, and matched in every particular against the archive copy of the same order. No successor government address could be established: three other J&K territorial hosts resolve and return no HTTP response from this environment, so whether the orders have been migrated is unknown.
caseFor: A government website being migrated, consolidated or allowed to lapse is common and unremarkable, and nothing here establishes intent, a takedown or a deliberate removal. Three J&K territorial hosts resolve without answering from this network position, so the orders may well be published today at an address this phase could not reach; the finding is bounded by one environment and one date. The documents themselves are not lost: the whole 2020 to 2025 series survives in the Internet Archive and the 2025 slice is live on a public server, and a retrieved copy is a retrieved copy whatever host served it. The Union also told Parliament in 2021 that its own orders are available on its own website, and that host is live.
caseAgainst: A compliance discharged by pointing at a URL is a compliance that ends when the URL does. The Union's answer to the Rajya Sabha in July 2022, on being asked whether it maintains data on J&K shutdowns, was to say the orders are uploaded on the official website of the Government of Jammu and Kashmir - and that website no longer resolves. So the documentary record of India's compliance with the Supreme Court's publication direction, for the territory the direction was made about, is currently preserved by a foundation in California and by a legal-services organisation in Delhi, and by no reachable government venue that this phase could find. It also disables every route: an absence route that names the Home Department's website is a placeholder route, and a placeholder route is worse than none.
assessmentNote: Filed no-objective because the record finds something real and no objective was stated at announcement against which it could be scored - no body announced anything about the venue, and there is no claim to test. The absence class also needs naming rather than forcing: these orders were collected, were published, and then became unreachable, which none of the four reasonKind values describes cleanly. On the schema's own producibility test the honest classification for the current state is not-published, with the history stated. They are not withheld: for the post-2020 series there is no named requester and no refusal, and treating unreachability as refusal would inflate the value.
caveat: The effect is stated and the cause is expressly not. An unresolvable host is not evidence of removal, and nothing here establishes that publication has ceased - only that the address the Union gave Parliament no longer exists.

title: Delimitation of Jammu and Kashmir: one Commission table, three denominators, three answers
summary: The Delimitation Commission's final order took effect on 20 May 2022, raising the Assembly from 83 fillable seats to 90 and allocating 47 to the Kashmir division and 43 to Jammu. On the 2011 Census population that leaves a Kashmir seat representing 21,481 more people than a Jammu seat, a gap of 17.17 per cent. On area it inverts: a Jammu seat covers 611.5 square kilometres against a Kashmir seat's 339.3. On the 2024 electoral roll the two divisions are within 1.31 per cent of each other. All three are computable from published official data, and the choice between them is the dispute.
claimAtLaunch: The statutory objective is that constituencies shall, so far as practicable, have equal population, having regard to physical features, existing boundaries of administrative units, means of communication and public convenience.
whatHappened: The seat chain, every step read from the Gazette: 111 seats in the erstwhile State Assembly including four in Ladakh, of which 24 were reserved for territory under Pakistan's occupation and never filled, leaving 87 that elections were actually held on. Section 14(3) of the Reorganisation Act set the new Assembly at 107 with section 14(4)(a) keeping 24 vacant - the Gazette spells 'twenty four' in words - which is 83; the Third Schedule was parsed entry by entry and contains exactly 83 constituencies numbered 1 to 83 with no gaps or duplicates, 46 in the Kashmir division and 37 in Jammu. Section 60(1) then raised 107 to 114, which is 90 fillable. Both arithmetics give the same seven: 90 minus 83 and 114 minus 107. The Commission sat from 6 March 2020 to 5 May 2022 and its two orders took effect on 20 May 2022 by an order of the Ministry of Law and Justice under section 62(2) and (3), not of the Home Ministry - which is why the Home Ministry's annual reports do not carry the date. The final allocation is 47 Kashmir and 43 Jammu, with 9 seats reserved for Scheduled Tribes and 7 for Scheduled Castes; the proportionality check on the Commission's own population header gives 9.35 and 6.78, so both round to what was allocated. The population arithmetic, with both ratios taken the same way round - Kashmir divided by Jammu - because taking them in opposite directions makes a widening gap read as a reversal: after delimitation, Kashmir's 6,888,475 over 47 seats is 146,563 per seat against Jammu's 5,378,538 over 43 at 125,082, a difference of 21,481 and a ratio of 1.1717. On the pre-delimitation frame of 46 and 37 the same populations give 149,749 and 145,366, a ratio of 1.0302. Both ratios exceed one, so a Kashmir seat represented more people than a Jammu seat before delimitation and represents more after; what changed is the size of the gap, from 3 per cent to 17 per cent. On area, Kashmir's 15,948 square kilometres over 47 seats is 339.3 and Jammu's 26,293 over 43 is 611.5. On the 2024 electoral roll, derived by summing the Commission's own phase press notes, Kashmir has 98,653 electors per seat and Jammu 97,377, a gap of 1.31 per cent - thirteen times smaller than the population gap, and the whole of the difference is that electors are 67.31 per cent of the Kashmir division's 2011 population against 77.85 per cent of Jammu's.
caseFor: The statute does not say population alone. Section 60 requires regard to physical features, existing boundaries of administrative units, means of communication and public convenience, and the Commission's own methodology says in terms that it weighted terrain, remoteness and border conditions alongside population. On area - which is what those factors are about - the allocation runs the other way, and a Jammu seat covers nearly twice the ground a Kashmir seat does. On the measure that actually determines representation at a poll, registered electors, the two divisions are within 1.31 per cent of each other, which is as close to parity as any delimitation in India achieves. The reservation of 9 seats for Scheduled Tribes was the first ever in the territory and is proportionate on the Commission's own population figures. And the Commission published the underlying table: population, area, density and seats, district by district, in adjacent columns, so both cases can be made from the body's own document.
caseAgainst: On the denominator the statute names first, the allocation moved in the wrong direction. Before delimitation a Kashmir seat represented 3 per cent more people than a Jammu seat; after it, 17 per cent more. A strict-proportional allocation on the Commission's own population figures gives the Kashmir division 50.54 seats against the 47 it received, and the Jammu division 39.46 against 43. The countervailing factors are not measured anywhere: the district categorisation that converts population and area into seats is the Commission's own judgement rather than a measurement, the tolerance band is stated as plus or minus 10 per cent in one place in the Commission's volume and plus or minus 20 per cent in another, and the additional constituency allowed for remoteness was granted under no published rule. The order is by section 60(5)(c) not to be called in question in any court. And the body that drew the constituencies contained nobody chosen by the population whose constituencies were drawn: its ex-officio members were the Chief Election Commissioner and a State Election Commissioner appointed by the administration of a Union Territory under President's rule, its five associate members from the Lok Sabha could by statute neither vote nor sign, and the Assembly half of its associate membership could not be constituted because the Assembly had been dissolved.
differentFactsNote: Flagged false deliberately, because the surface of this dispute - region against region, census against census - makes it look like a different-facts case and it is not. Both cases rest on the same table, Working Paper I of the Delimitation Commission's own compendium, and disagree only about which column of it is the right denominator. On 2011 population the Kashmir division is under-allocated by 3.54 seats and a Jammu seat represents 21,481 fewer people; on area the Jammu division is under-allocated by 13 seats; on the 2024 electoral roll the disparity is 1.31 per cent. All three computations are exact, all three use figures published by official bodies, and the first two use figures the Commission itself printed in adjacent columns of one page. Granting either side's strongest fact in full leaves the other's intact, so criterion (b) passes - but criterion (c) fails decisively, because the common ledger was not merely constructible, it was constructed here in a few lines of arithmetic from published data. An unbuilt comparison fails (c); a built one fails it more clearly. The problem is not the absence of a common measure but an embarrassment of them, none of which any party committed to in advance.
assessmentNote: Filed contested, and the value is carrying a weighting dispute rather than an evidentiary one, which is recorded here rather than resolved. On the written definition the evidence supports more than one defensible reading and this record does not choose between them, which fits - but the more precise description is that it supports one reading of the facts and three of their weight. no-objective is wrong because an objective was stated in the statute; failed and partly both presuppose a single denominator the statute does not supply. This is the L-0092 shape - a finding about how a figure is presented and what it is presented against - and it should be reviewed with L-0092. No new enum value is proposed.

title: Turnout in Jammu and Kashmir: four official values for one quantity, and a denominator nobody publishes
summary: The Election Commission published four different turnout figures for the same 2024 Lok Sabha quantity in Jammu and Kashmir, and disclosed in a chart footnote that its own 'highest in 35 years' comparison puts its final point on a different basis from every earlier one. For the 2024 assembly election it has published no statistical report at all - and none for any of the eight state assemblies polled that year - so the denominator behind its headline 63.88 per cent is nowhere stated. Reconstructed from the Commission's own phase press notes, it is 8,823,899 registered electors across 90 constituencies.
whatHappened: Four official values for one quantity, all the Commission's own and all retrieved: 58.46 per cent as combined turnout at the polling stations for the five Lok Sabha seats, in a press release of 27 May 2024; 58.58 per cent quoted as the same election's turnout in a release of 3 October 2024; 58.07 per cent computed from the statistical report's own electors and EVM votes, excluding the 50,999 postal ballots; and 58.65 per cent, the statistical report's own printed State Total, postal-inclusive. The pattern repeats seat by seat, and two of the five move down rather than up between press note and statistical report, so it is not simply provisional plus postal. The Commission states the basis break itself, in a footnote under its own chart: the graph depicts gross turnout for 1996 to 2019 and, for 2024, turnout at polling stations. A further inconsistency inside the same report family has not been stated anywhere: in 2014 the assembly report's headline excludes postal ballots and the Lok Sabha report's headline includes them - one year, one territory, two definitions of turnout, neither cross-referenced. The consequence for the live corpus is that the 65.91 per cent recorded for the 2014 assembly election is the postal-inclusive figure and the widely quoted 65.52 per cent is the at-polling-stations figure, and both are printed in the same Commission document seven pages apart; neither is wrong and neither should be corrected to the other. For 2024 the equivalent cannot be computed at all, because the assembly statistical report does not exist. The denominator was reconstructed by summing the registered-elector column of the Commission's three phase press notes, which between them cover assembly constituencies 1 to 90 exactly once with no gaps and no duplicates - 2,327,580 plus 2,578,099 plus 3,918,220 - and the reconstruction validates itself: weighting the ninety constituency turnouts by their own elector counts reproduces the Commission's published 63.88 per cent to four significant figures. Division-wise, Kashmir polled 55.50 per cent and Jammu 73.15 per cent, a gap of 17.65 percentage points, with individual Srinagar-city constituencies as low as 19.81 per cent against 81.47 per cent in a Jammu seat. One further item is recorded as what was said rather than as what it meant, because nothing more can be established: on 17 August 2022 the Chief Electoral Officer of J&K, Hirdesh Kumar, spoke at Jammu about expected additions to the electoral roll, two press renderings of the figure disagree with each other, and on 20 August 2022 the J&K Information Department described the reporting as a misrepresentation of facts. That is a contradiction issued by the executive, not a retraction by the speaker, and the distinction must be kept. No primary text was retrievable: the Chief Electoral Officer's own host resolves and refuses connections. The only hard number in the vicinity is the elector count itself, which on the post-2019 territory grew from 7,743,306 at the 2019 General Election to 8,802,348 at the 2024 one, a rise of 1,059,042 or 13.68 per cent in five years - and that figure is evidence for no characterisation of who was added.
caseFor: The four values are four stated bases for one quantity, not four attempts at a single number, and each is printed with the basis it rests on: turnout at polling stations, gross turnout, and postal-inclusive and postal-exclusive totals are different measures that different users need, and a body publishing only one of them would be criticised for that instead. The basis break in the long comparison was disclosed by the Commission itself, in a footnote to the chart carrying the comparison, which is not the behaviour of an institution concealing a discontinuity - the 1996-to-2019 series and the 2024 point are labelled as different bases on the same page. The 2014 pair the corpus records is the clearest case: 65.52 and 65.91 are both printed in the Commission's own document, seven pages apart, each under its own heading, and neither is a correction of the other. For 2024 the constituency-level components were published within days of each phase, in enough detail that a reader can assemble the total the report has not yet printed. And the missing assembly statistical report is absent for all eight states polled in 2024, which places it in the Commission's publication schedule rather than in anything specific to this territory.
caseAgainst: A turnout percentage without its denominator is not a figure a reader can use, and for the 2024 assembly election the Commission has published no denominator anywhere - the total had to be rebuilt from ninety rows scattered across three press notes. Twenty-two months after the poll there is still no published figure for electors, votes polled including postal, valid votes, NOTA, rejected votes or constituency-wise turnout on the final basis. Four official values for one Lok Sabha quantity, two of which move in opposite directions between documents, mean that any comparison of J&K turnout across years inherits whichever basis its source happened to pick, and almost every secondary account is derived from a Commission press note rather than from a Commission report. The Commission's own press note of 1 October 2024 states that constituencies increased 'from 83 in 2014 to 90 in 2024', when the 2014 election was held on 87 constituencies on the authority of the Commission's own statistical report for that election - 83 is the post-Ladakh, pre-delimitation count on which no election was ever held. That is a retroactive relabelling in an official release, and it is the figure the secondary literature quotes.
assessmentNote: Filed no-objective because the record is a finding about a measuring instrument and no objective was stated at announcement against which the instrument could be scored. The Election Commission announces no turnout target and makes no claim about what its basis is beyond what its documents print. The value asserts nothing about the finding's quality: every figure here is from a retrieved Commission document and every identity in the reconstruction closes.

title: Five nominated seats in the J&K Assembly, and a statute that never says whether they vote
summary: The Reorganisation Act allowed the Lieutenant Governor to nominate two women members if he is of opinion that women are not adequately represented. An amendment in force from 26 December 2023 added three more nominated seats - two for Kashmiri Migrants, one of whom must be a woman, and one for a person displaced from Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir. All five sit outside the directly elected total. None of the provisions says anything about the rights, powers, privileges or voting entitlement of a nominated member, and none has yet been exercised.
claimAtLaunch: The Government's own account of its own Bill, in a press release of 6 December 2023, describes the measure five times as reservation - 'reservation of 2 seats', '1 seat to be reserved' - and states that by giving reservation to displaced Kashmiris they will have a voice in the Assembly.
whatHappened: Sections 15, 15A and 15B are single-sentence enabling provisions each hinged on a 'notwithstanding section 14(3)' clause, which is what places the nominated seats outside the directly elected total. All three are silent on powers. The Government's own arithmetic, given on the floor and carried in the same release: earlier there were 107 seats and 2 nominated members, now there are 114 seats and 5. The Delimitation Commission recommended two numbered things - at least two members from the Kashmiri Migrant community, and that they have power at par with the equivalent members in another Union Territory with a legislature. Parliament enacted the first and not the second, and inverted it in the same clause: 'at least two' became 'not more than two'. So the recommendation drafted to close the rights question in advance was halved and reversed, and what was enacted is silent. As at 3 August 2026 no nomination has been made under any of the three sections: the Assembly's own live member directory shows ninety honourable members and, on its own filter for nominated members, zero. A power created in December 2023 and litigated over since 2024 has never been exercised. The gap is being litigated rather than legislated: a petition challenging the three sections is before the High Court on the pleaded assumption that the nominated members have full voting rights, and the Union's answer on the relayed account defends the Lieutenant Governor's discretion to nominate without addressing voting at all - so the two sides in the only live proceeding are not joined on the question. And the government's own account of its own Bill uses the word the Bill does not: a reserved seat is filled by election within a defined electorate and its holder has an elected member's rights, while a nominated seat is filled by discretion and carries no stated rights at all. Separately, two official sources four and a half months apart give different sizes for the registered Kashmiri Migrant population that is the gateway to two of the seats - 46,517 families and 158,976 persons in the Bill's own Statement of Objects and Reasons, 46,631 families and 157,967 persons in the Government's account of the Home Minister's reply. Families rose while persons fell, which cannot happen by accretion, and neither figure carries an as-at date or a note.
caseFor: Nomination is a recognised device in Indian legislatures for constituencies that geography cannot deliver, and this is the case it was designed for. Kashmiri Migrants displaced from the Valley are dispersed across camps and cities outside the territory they would vote in, and persons displaced from Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir have no seat that answers to them; neither group can be reached by redrawing a boundary, which is the only tool delimitation has. Parliament has used nomination for exactly this before - for Anglo-Indians in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies until 2020, and in the Union Territory of Puducherry, whose nominated members the courts have held sit on the same footing as elected ones. The Delimitation Commission, whose recommendation the Act follows, arrived at the same instrument. On the voting question the Act's silence is not obviously a denial: section 22 expressly withholds a vote from Ministers who are not members and from the Advocate-General, so the statute demonstrates it knows how to exclude and did not do so here, and the Puducherry line reads such silence in favour of the vote. The women's provision is narrower still - conditional on the Lieutenant Governor forming an opinion that women are not adequately represented, which is a threshold to be satisfied and not a standing power.
caseAgainst: The central question - whether five members the Lieutenant Governor may appoint at his discretion can vote in a ninety-member House - is not answered anywhere in the enacted law, and the silence is not an oversight that can be read past: the Commission's recommendation was drafted to close it and Parliament legislated around it. On the relayed account the Union's own position in the litigation is that the power is exercisable by the Lieutenant Governor in his discretion, without the aid and advice of the elected government, which makes the size of the House partly a matter for an appointee of the Union. The textual argument against reading the silence as a denial of the vote appears not to have been made anywhere and is strong: the same Act expressly denies a vote to Ministers who are not members and to the Advocate-General in section 22, and section 25(1) decides questions by a majority of members present and voting. The Act knows how to withhold a vote and did not withhold this one - which makes the silence in sections 15, 15A and 15B a legislative choice against a background of explicit exclusions elsewhere in the same statute. The Government's own promotional account of the Bill calls the seats reservation five times, which is the word that implies the rights the Bill does not confer. And the register that is the operative gateway to two of the seats has two different official sizes four and a half months apart, moving in opposite directions on its two counts, with no as-at date and no reconciliation on either.
assessmentNote: Filed awaiting-adjudication on the written definition and it fits on all three limbs: the provisions are in force from 26 December 2023, the central question they raise - whether five members the Lieutenant Governor may appoint can vote in a ninety-member House - is testable in principle, and the term that would settle it is a pending decision by a body outside the enacting authority, in a petition adjourned repeatedly since 2024. Elapsed time is not the obstacle, which is why too-early does not describe it. One presentational finding sits inside this record without being its subject: the statute says "nominate" and the Government's account of it says "reserve" five times.
caveat: The litigation chronology and the Union's affidavit in the pending challenge are relayed through search extraction and press pages: no document from that proceeding was retrieved and none may be quoted as primary. The comparator judgment is no longer in that class - K. Lakshminarayanan v. Union of India was retrieved in full from the Supreme Court's own host on 3 August 2026 and is cited as T1.

unmeasured.what: Whether a nominated member of the J&K Legislative Assembly may vote
unmeasured.why: Sections 15, 15A and 15B say nothing about the rights, powers, privileges or voting entitlement of a nominated member, and nothing elsewhere in the Reorganisation Act as retrieved or in the Amendment Act as retrieved supplies a powers clause. There is no agreed definition of what a nominated seat in this Assembly is, so the question cannot be answered from the enacted law at all - and it is not that nobody has considered it, since the Delimitation Commission's recommendation was drafted to close the gap by borrowing another Union Territory's settled position and Parliament did not enact that borrowing. No route is invented, because closing this requires either a legislative amendment or a judgment.

unmeasured.what: Whether the Lieutenant Governor has formed the opinion section 15 requires, that women are not adequately represented

title: Permanent resident replaced by domicile: a definitional change, and the sub-count the Union did not publish for five years
summary: The category of permanent resident, which had defined who could hold immovable property, take State employment and claim State scholarships in Jammu and Kashmir, was replaced by a domicile category defined by executive order in 2020. The Union published a total of certificates issued and, once, the number issued to people who already held or depended on a permanent-resident certificate. The complement - certificates to people who did not - was never published by the Union, and appeared only when a restored J&K Assembly asked for it in April 2025.
whatHappened: The Union's published figures, every one prefaced 'As per the information provided by the Government of Jammu & Kashmir'. Around September 2020, with no as-on date stated: 2,113,879 applications received, 1,679,520 certificates issued, 121,630 rejected. As on 31 December 2020, given twice in identical terms in March 2021: 3,544,938 applications, 3,231,353 issued, 215,438 rejected, and 3,108,682 issued to dependents or holders of erstwhile Permanent Resident Certificates. The residual, 3,231,353 minus 3,108,682, is 122,671 - and it is not a count of newcomers. It necessarily mixes persons qualifying on the migrant limb, children of central-government officials, children of parents who qualify, and persons who were entitled to a permanent-resident certificate but never held one in their own name, because the published denominator is certificate-holding rather than entitlement. Treating it as a count of outsiders granted domicile would be exactly the laundering this instrument exists to prevent. A further 98,147 applications on the same date were neither issued nor rejected; that subtraction is derived here and is stated in no reply. Then the Union series stops. A sweep of every parliamentary answer published on the Ministry's own day-pages for 2019 to 2026 - 3,674 files - finds the word domicile in no answer after 24 March 2021. Five and a half years of sessions have produced no update. The quantity the Union did not disaggregate was produced within months of the J&K Assembly resuming: in April 2025 the Revenue Minister told a member that 83,742 domicile certificates had been granted to persons described as non-state subjects in the preceding two years, out of roughly 3.512 million issued in that period. That figure is relayed and carries three cautions: the assembly reply itself could not be reached; 'non-state subject' is the reply's own pre-2019 term and is not obviously the complement of the Union's 'dependents or holders of erstwhile Permanent Resident Certificates'; and its period is roughly 2023 to 2025, so it must not be added to or subtracted from the 2020 residual, and the gap between them remains unpublished.
caseFor: The permanent-resident category was itself an exclusion, and the people it excluded are identifiable and were excluded for generations: West Pakistan refugees, Valmikis and Gorkhas resident in the territory for decades could not hold immovable property, could not take State employment, and could not claim State scholarships, and a woman who married a person from outside lost her status. Replacing a hereditary status with a residence-and-study test extends to those populations rights every other Indian citizen already held, and it does so on conditions - long residence, or schooling in the territory - that are ordinary in Indian domicile law. The scale of the exercise is also evidence against the fear it was designed to serve: 3.1 million of the 3.2 million certificates issued to the end of 2020 went to people who already held or depended on a permanent-resident certificate, which is a conversion of existing status rather than an influx.
caseAgainst: The definition of who belongs to a territory was replaced by executive order, under a power that expired within a year of the appointed day, at a time when the legislature of that territory did not exist and could not be consulted. And the one quantity that would let anyone test what the change did - certificates issued to persons who were not previously permanent residents - was not published by the Union in five and a half years, while the Union's own answers show the underlying split was separable from the start, since it published the complement in 2020. That the figure existed all along is now established rather than inferred: a restored Assembly asked and got 83,742 within months. The Union's own series then simply stops in March 2021, so there is no published Union figure for anything after 31 December 2020, and a reader looking at the published record cannot tell whether that is because nothing happened or because nobody asked.
differentFactsNote: The two sides do not share a measure, and the failure is structural rather than clerical. The case for rests on legal-status facts - that named populations resident for generations could not hold property, take State employment or claim scholarships, and that a woman marrying a non-resident lost status. Those are facts about who was excluded from a category, and the excluded population was never enumerated by any instrument: there is no stock count of permanent residents anywhere, and the object 'person who held permanent-resident status and did not convert' has no agreed definition at all, because the two statuses have different qualifying conditions and neither population is enumerated as a stock. The case against rests on process facts - that the definition was replaced by executive order under a power that expired within a year, when the affected legislature did not exist. Granting the government's 3,108,682 in full leaves the process objection untouched; granting the process objection in full leaves the rights-extension case untouched. The one quantity that would join them, certificates by year and by qualifying limb, is not published, and the only figure that exists is on a different period under a different category name. That is criterion (c) in its stated form: a constitutional process against a stated absence, crossing a category boundary.
assessmentNote: Filed contested on the written definition: the evidence supports more than one defensible reading and this record does not choose between them. It is not partly or failed, because no objective was stated at announcement for the domicile order that could be scored, and it is not no-objective, because both sides are making claims about effects that the record has to weigh rather than merely reporting an unclaimed finding.

title: Land law repealed by executive order five days before the power lapsed, and a transfer count in four units
summary: The land laws of Jammu and Kashmir were repealed and amended by executive order on 26 October 2020, five days before the one-year adaptation power in the Reorganisation Act expired, and at a time when the territory had no legislature. The Union then published the number of persons from outside the territory who bought land there five times in five years, in four different units, and stopped in April 2023. The area involved was published by nobody until a restored Assembly asked in October 2025.
whatHappened: The instrument is commonly misattributed and the citation matters: the gazette issue of 26 October 2020 contains two orders back to back, and the land repeals and amendments are all in the Adaptation of State Laws Fifth Order, whose schedule is 26 State Acts - not in the Adaptation of Central Laws Third Order published beside it, whose schedule is three central Acts including the real estate regulation statute. The Union's published counts of purchases by persons from outside the Union Territory, each prefaced 'As per the information provided by the Government of Jammu and Kashmir': August 2021, two persons and two properties since August 2019; December 2021, seven plots of land, with no period stated at all and all seven in the Jammu division; March 2022, 34 persons after the abrogation of Article 370, in four named districts; April 2023, 185 persons over calendar 2020, 2021 and 2022, split 1, 57 and 127, with Ladakh separately recording none. Four units in five answers - properties, plots, persons, and then persons with area and value - and the levels do not reconcile across them: two persons since August 2019 in one answer against 57 persons in calendar 2021 alone in another, both official, both sourced to the same producer, with no document saying whether the object narrowed or the base was silently revised. Then the Union series stops: the same exhaustive sweep of 3,674 answer PDFs finds no J&K land-purchase figure in any Ministry answer after April 2023. In October 2025 the J&K Assembly was told 631 non-residents had bought 386 kanal worth 129.97 crore rupees since October 2019, split 378 persons and 212 kanal 13 marla in Jammu against 253 persons and 173 kanal 7 marla in Kashmir. Those figures reconcile internally: the persons sum, the value sums, and the area sums exactly at twenty marla to the kanal. The relayed year-by-year breakdown does not reconcile - the years available give 512 against a stated 631, leaving 119 unaccounted which must be the 2019 stub plus 2023, and no outlet prints 2023, so 2023 must not be reconstructed by subtraction. In comparable units 386 kanal is 48.25 acres, about 19.5 hectares, or 0.00046 per cent of the Union Territory's 42,241 square kilometres.
caseFor: The quantity that dominates the argument is not the quantity that dominates the land. Over roughly the same window in which 19.5 hectares passed to persons from outside the territory, the Ministry told Parliament that 2,359 hectares of State land had been acquired for public purposes across all twenty districts and that central agencies had acquired a further 332 hectares in Kashmir alone for national highways and similar projects - so private transfer to outsiders is about one part in 216,000 of the territory and a small fraction of what the state itself took for public works. The definitional point cuts the same way and harder: on a single relayed account roughly 350 of the 631 counted non-resident buyers are people from Ladakh, chiefly from Kargil, who were residents of the same State before 31 October 2019 and are outsiders now only because an administrative boundary moved. And the Union did answer, five times, whenever it was asked.
caseAgainst: The land law of a territory was rewritten by executive notification, five days before the power to do so expired, with no legislature in existence to be consulted, and the Union's own answer of December 2019 concedes that land and property are subjects for that legislature. The counting that followed cannot support any trend claim: four units across five answers, one of them a stock with no clock, and two official figures that cannot both describe the same object. The Union series then terminates in April 2023 and the area - the denominator both sides would accept - was published by nobody until a different legislature asked in 2025. And there is one undertaking on the record that was never performed: asked in December 2021 for the details of commercial land deals, the Ministry answered that the information was being collected and would be laid on the Table of the House, and no subsequent answer lays it.
differentFactsNote: Flagged false and noted, because the temptation to mark it true comes from the units disagreeing across answers, and that is an instrument defect rather than a property of the argument. Both sides are talking about the same underlying quantity - land transferred to persons from outside the territory - and disagree about its weight and its trajectory rather than about its value. The common ledger is land area, which both sides accept, and it is not merely constructible: as of October 2025 it has actually been built, because the assembly reply reports the same event set in persons, area and value simultaneously. 386 kanal against 42,241 square kilometres is a single measure on which both claims can be laid. An unbuilt comparison fails criterion (c); this one is not even unbuilt. What divides the two sides is whether a small stock is evidence of a small flow or of an early one, and whether the counted category means what its name says.
assessmentNote: Filed contested on the written definition. Two defensible readings of the same figures are available - a negligible transfer largely composed of people from the erstwhile same State, and an early stock under an instrument whose counting cannot support any statement about trajectory - and this record does not choose between them.

title: The third tier in Jammu and Kashmir was elected once, and every elected term has since lapsed with no successor election
summary: Jammu and Kashmir had no constitutionally grounded third tier until 2019, because Parts IX and IXA did not apply to it. Since then panchayats, Block Development Councils, municipal bodies and a new directly elected District Development Council in every district have all been elected. All of them have also expired: the municipal bodies in October and November 2023, the panchayats and BDCs on 9 January 2024, and the District Development Councils on 24 February 2026. Not one successor election has been held.
claimAtLaunch: The Ministry of Home Affairs' Annual Report for 2021-22 records 27 functions transferred to the Panchayati Raj Institutions and approximately 1,727 crore rupees devolved to them, and 17 of the 18 functions in the Twelfth Schedule devolved to the urban tier with funds and functionaries, 2,300 crore rupees devolved over two years and 3,160 works completed with 3,200 ongoing, geo-tagged and published.
whatHappened: The 2018 panchayat election left the tier a third empty on the administration's own figures: 22,214 panches and 3,459 sarpanches were elected against 33,592 panch and 4,290 sarpanch constituencies, so 12,209 of 37,882 seats - 32.2 per cent - were unfilled on the day the results were declared. By November 2020 the administration's own statistics table put vacancies at 13,241, and its divisional and grand totals reproduce exactly on re-addition. Of the 1,032-seat increase the administration names the causes as death, resignation and 'etc' and quantifies exactly one of them: 307 seats fell vacant when Block Development Council chairpersons were elected in October 2019. That leaves 725 seats emptied by death, resignation and something else, unquantified by cause in the issuing authority's own document. The turnout figure describes a minority of the seats, and the election authority said so itself - but only from its sixth press release onward. Its first five releases report that the State witnessed a polling percentage of 74.1, 71.1, 75.2, 71.3 and 71.1 per cent, with no qualifier; from 3 December 2018 the same authority reports turnout 'in respect of the Sarpanch and Panch constituencies that have seen contests', and that wording never leaves. Over the seven phases whose releases survive, covering 76 per cent of the pre-break state, 41.6 per cent of seats went to a poll, 25.1 per cent were filled unopposed, and 33.3 per cent had no candidate at all; in the Kashmir valley 708 of 2,135 halqas had no candidate and 699 had exactly one, and two districts saw no polling whatever. The District Development Council was built in a single year - amendment on 16 and 17 October 2020, delimitation notified 26 October, reservation notified 3 November, polls from 28 November, results 22 December - and gave every one of the twenty districts fourteen constituencies, 280 seats in all, with statutory reservation for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and women. Then all three tiers lapsed. Article 243E and Article 243U require elections to be completed before the expiry of a body's duration; officials were installed instead - Block Development Officers over the panchayats for six months or till further orders, and Commissioners over the municipal corporations under a removal-of-difficulties clause. The stated reasons have rotated for more than two years: delimitation, then reservation for Other Backward Classes, then a commission whose report has awaited approval for a year, then a vacant State Election Commissioner's post, then a fresh revision of the rolls.
caseFor: For seventy years the territory had no constitutionally grounded third tier at all: Parts IX and IXA did not apply, panchayat elections were run not by an independent State Election Commission but by the state's own Chief Electoral Officer acting as an Election Authority, and even that machinery was used so intermittently that the panchayats elected in 2011 were the first in a decade and the urban bodies elected in 2005 lapsed in 2010 and stayed vacant for eight years. Since 2019 elections have been held at all three rural tiers and at the urban tier. A directly elected District Development Council now exists in every district, with statutory reservation for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and women - and most Indian states have no directly elected district tier at all, so this is a genuine institutional advance over the district planning boards it replaced. Turnout in the 2020 council polls was substantially better than the 2018 panchayat polls in the valley, with Srinagar district recording about 35 per cent against 14.5 per cent in the panchayat poll and 7.9 per cent in the 2019 parliamentary poll. Parliament has since legislated reservation for Other Backward Classes into all three local-bodies statutes and supplied a statutory removal procedure for the State Election Commissioner. The present interval is an interval being worked through: the reservation commission reported in February 2025, delimitation is complete for 72 of 77 urban bodies, the panchayat roll has been revised, and a new State Election Commissioner took office in February 2026.
caseAgainst: A tier that was elected once. The headline turnout for the 2018 panchayat election is computed over the seats that saw a contest - the authority's own words from its sixth release onward, having presented the same kind of figure without that qualifier five times before - and over the phases whose releases survive, two seats in five went to a poll and a third had no candidate at all. A number computed over two seats in five and presented without its denominator is not a measure of participation but a measure of the places that participated. The tier those elections created was never full: nearly a third of its seats were empty on the day of the result, the figure had risen by November 2020, and the administration's own note quantifies one cause of the increase and leaves 725 seats to death, resignation and 'etc'. A vacancy series that cannot distinguish a seat nobody stood for from a seat whose holder was killed is not a vacancy series. And the tier has now stopped existing at every level, in the face of two constitutional articles requiring elections to be completed before expiry, with officials installed in place of the elected. The tier holds no measure of itself either: the one published devolution figure appeared in a single annual report and has not been repeated, its rural half was given without a denominator while its urban half was given with one, and there is no State Finance Commission report and no local-bodies audit anywhere in the record.
differentFactsNote: Flagged false, and it fails on the second precondition as well as the third, which is unusual and is the cleaner test. The two sides cite the same tables and divide them differently: the turnout figure the case for uses and the excluded-seats figure the case against uses come out of the same seven press releases, and the common ledger - seats going to poll, seats unopposed, seats with no candidate, and the electorate attached to each - was constructed here in about a dozen subtractions from published data. Both sides also accept 22,214 panches and 3,459 sarpanches elected of 33,592 and 4,290, and neither disputes that 280 council seats were filled in December 2020 or that the term expired on 24 February 2026. But precondition (b) fails too: granting the case for's strongest fact in full - a directly elected district tier with women's and tribal reservation, more than most states have - does not leave the case against intact, because the case against's core claim is that this tier's term has expired with no election held, and that is a claim about the same tier. These are not parallel facts but successive states of one object. The one place a category boundary is genuinely crossed is the devolution argument, a quantity against a stated absence - and it fails criterion (c) for the ordinary reason, that a funds-released-and-spent series for this tier is unbuilt rather than unbuildable.
assessmentNote: Scored partly, and the objective being scored is declared here because no field holds it: the stated objective is the one in the Ministry's own Annual Report - a functioning three-tier elected local government with functions, funds and functionaries devolved - read together with Articles 243E and 243U, which require elections to be completed before a body's duration expires. Part of that was achieved: elections were held at every tier between 2018 and 2020, a district tier was created that most states do not have, and reservation was legislated. It was not sustained: every elected term has now lapsed without a successor election. contested was considered and rejected, because the facts are not in dispute between the two sides - what happened is agreed and only its weight is argued - and because the case against's central claim directly contradicts the implication of the case for rather than sitting beside it.

unmeasured.why: The best-evidenced absence in the subject, and it is not merely that records probably exist. Section 8(1) of the Panchayati Raj Act makes the cause of a vacancy and its duration a statutory element: a vacancy occurring by death or resignation is filled by election or nomination provided it is for a period of more than six months, so the holder cannot act on a vacancy without determining which limb it falls under and how long it has run. The information is therefore not merely producible under compulsion, it is statutorily required to exist before the by-election the administration describes can be called - and the department annexed halqa-wise and constituency-wise lists of vacant seats to its own orders. What is published is a total with one of its causes quantified and 725 seats left to death, resignation and 'etc'. No named requester and no refusal, so it is not withheld.

title: The J&K local tier has no State Finance Commission report, no local-bodies audit, and its Finance Commission grants fell to zero and then stopped appearing
summary: Jammu and Kashmir enacted a State Finance Commission Act in 2011 requiring a commission to be constituted as soon as may be and every fifth year thereafter. No document establishes that any such commission was ever constituted, reported or had its report acted on. The Comptroller and Auditor General's own database returns zero local-bodies audit reports for the territory as either State or Union Territory, while returning them for other states. And the Ministry of Panchayati Raj's own devolution index scores the territory at 27.85 against a national average of 43.89. And the Union's own Finance Commission grants to the territory's Gram Panchayats were released at 53.64 per cent of allocation across the 2015-20 award, with the whole of the final year's 1,049.49 crore rupees released at zero - after which the territory has no row at all in the successor award's allocation table.
whatHappened: The J&K State Finance Commission for Panchayats and Municipalities Act 2011 received assent on 23 April 2011 and was brought into force on 24 June 2011. Section 3(1) requires the Government to constitute a commission as soon as may be and thereafter at the expiration of every fifth year; section 10 gives it the tax-sharing, assignment and grants-in-aid functions the Constitution assigns to a State Finance Commission; section 12 requires it to submit its report to the Government within the time prescribed. There the chain stops. A full-text search of the Act for 'laid', 'laying', 'lay before' and 'action taken' returns nothing but a good-faith protection clause: the Act contains no provision requiring the report to be laid before the legislature with an action-taken memorandum, which is the mechanism the Constitution supplies for States. A Government of J&K committee report of 2011, chaired by the Chief Secretary, records that the Panchayati Raj Act has no provision for a State Finance Commission and recommends that one be formed as early as possible - so none had been constituted then. And a study of the latest State Finance Commission report of every State, commissioned by the Sixteenth Finance Commission itself and published in June 2025, covers 28 States including two whose only commission is a first-generation one, and does not mention Jammu and Kashmir anywhere. The honest limit is stated: that study covers States, and the territory's absence is partly explained by its Union Territory status - but no document was found establishing that a J&K commission was ever constituted, reported, tabled or answered. On audit, the Comptroller and Auditor General's own search form confirms the territorial break independently, offering separate entries for the State up to 30 October 2019 and the Union Territory from 31 October 2019 onward. Filtering that database for local-bodies audit reports returns zero results for the territory on either entry. Both controls hold: the same filter without the territory returns local-bodies reports for other states, and the territory without the filter returns ten reports including audits of Union Territory finances and revenues. On devolution, the Ministry of Panchayati Raj's index for 2024 scores the territory 23.07 on framework, 11.88 on functions, 13.29 on finances, 36.97 on functionaries, 55.08 on capacity enhancement and 39.76 on accountability, for an overall 27.85, against national averages of 54.29, 29.18, 37.04, 50.96, 54.63, 47.51 and 43.89. So the territory stands at 63.5 per cent of the national average overall, 42.5 per cent on framework, 40.7 per cent on functions and 35.9 per cent on finances. No rank is stated here: the published table gives scores and the ranking that circulates is a computation, not a published figure. On grants, from a written answer to the Lok Sabha of 9 December 2025 carrying two annexures. Annexure-I gives Fourteenth Finance Commission grants to Gram Panchayats in Jammu and Kashmir, allocation against release, in rupees crore: 373.96 and 367.72 in 2015-16, 585.73 and 474.41, 675.15 and 470.97, 779.40 and 544.83, and 1,049.49 against 0.00 in 2019-20 - totalling 3,463.73 allocated and 1,857.93 released, and both column sums were re-added independently and match the printed totals. Two figures that follow are derived here and are stated nowhere in the answer: unreleased 1,605.80 crore rupees, and an overall release rate of 53.64 per cent. The per-year release rates, also computed here, fall monotonically before the zero - 98.3, then 81.0, then 69.8, then 69.9 per cent - so the final year terminates a declining series rather than interrupting a healthy one. Two facts coincide in that final year and nothing retrieved connects them: the appointed day fell on 31 October 2019, seven months into it, so the State the award named ceased to exist part-way through; and the release was zero. Annexure-II of the same answer gives the Fifteenth Finance Commission's allocation and release to Rural Local Bodies as at 2 December 2025 for 28 States and no Union Territories, and Jammu and Kashmir has no row - the list runs straight from Himachal Pradesh to Jharkhand. The Ministry's own description of the mechanism, in a separate release, is that it recommends release of these grants to States. The legal basis for the exclusion is not established: the Commission's main-report provisions for Union Territories could not be retrieved, and the account in circulation that resources for the new Union Territories were adjusted from the Centre's own share is relayed and was never retrieved, so it is not used here to explain the gap.
caseFor: Some of this is a consequence of status rather than of neglect. Article 243-I binds States and Governors, and the study that omits Jammu and Kashmir omits every Union Territory, so its silence is not evidence that the territory failed a duty the Constitution places on it. The devolution index itself records that a State Finance Commission is excluded from its framework dimension because all States have constituted at least a first-generation one and no State can be disqualified on that factor - a sentence that is about States, and the territory is scored as a Union Territory. On the two dimensions that measure what local bodies can actually do rather than what they are entitled to, the territory scores closest to the national average: 55.08 on capacity enhancement against 54.63, which is above it. And the territory has been rebuilding its third tier from nothing since 2019, which is a short period in which to construct a fiscal architecture. On grants, the shortfall is neither new nor unexplained in principle. Finance Commission local-body grants are conditional on reforms the Commission states on the face of its own report - notified property-tax floor rates, accounts available online both before and after audit at individual, State and all-India level, and accounting-system reform - with transfer required within ten working days and interest payable on delay. A territory with no published local-bodies audit and no State Finance Commission report does not meet them. And the precedent has a stated cause: under the Twelfth Finance Commission 281 crore rupees was earmarked for the territory's panchayati raj institutions and 228 crore of it, 81 per cent, could not be secured for non-fulfilment of prescribed conditions - a shortfall proportionally worse than the 2015-20 award's, under a State government, long before the reorganisation.
caseAgainst: The territory has its own Act, passed in 2011, requiring a commission as soon as may be and every fifth year after - and fifteen years later no document anywhere establishes that one was ever constituted. Its own Chief Secretary's committee said in 2011 that none existed and recommended one be formed as early as possible. The Act as drafted also omits the very mechanism that gives a finance commission force: there is no requirement that the report be laid before the legislature with an action-taken memorandum, so even a report that existed would carry no obligation to be answered. The Comptroller and Auditor General's own database returns nothing at all for local bodies in the territory, on either side of the reorganisation, while returning reports for other states on the same query - so the third tier is unaudited as well as unfunded by any published formula. And the Ministry's own index puts the territory at 35.9 per cent of the national average on finances, the dimension the missing commission exists to govern. And the money did not merely fall short - it stopped. Across the 2015-20 award 1,605.80 crore rupees of 3,463.73 allocated was never released, the release rate declining every single year, and the whole of the final year's 1,049.49 crore, the largest allocation of the award, was released at nothing. Then the territory disappears from the instrument altogether: the Ministry's own table of Fifteenth Finance Commission allocations to rural local bodies lists 28 States and Jammu and Kashmir is not among them, so there is no successor figure to fall short of. A tier with no finance commission of its own, no audit, no published devolution measure and no line in the national local-body grant table is not underfunded on a measure - it is absent from the measure.
assessmentNote: Filed no-objective because the record finds something real about an institutional architecture and no objective was stated at announcement against which it could be scored. The 2011 Act states a duty rather than an objective, and no body has announced a target for constituting a commission, for auditing the local tier, or for a devolution score. The value asserts nothing about the finding's quality: the Act, the 2011 committee report, the Sixteenth Finance Commission's own commissioned study, the audit database queries with both controls, and the index table were all retrieved and read.
