title: The J&K human rights commission was abolished, and the body said to replace it cannot investigate the respondents its caseload named
summary: The Jammu and Kashmir State Human Rights Commission was extinguished on the appointed day with more than 630 complaints pending, and the National Human Rights Commission acquired ordinary jurisdiction over the territory for the first time. Complaints registered with the national body from J&K have risen from 210 in the last full pre-break year to 982 in 2023-24. Referrals from the national body to a state commission, which ran at 38 and 51 in the two preceding years, have been zero in every year since. And section 19 of the national Act, untouched by the reorganisation, bars the national Commission from investigating the armed forces - the class of respondent the abolished Commission's caseload most often named.
whatHappened: The Fifth Schedule did two things to the human rights architecture on one day. Table-1 entry 86 omitted the proviso that had kept the central Protection of Human Rights Act out of the erstwhile State for matters on the State List, so the national Commission gained ordinary jurisdiction. Table-3 entry 117 repealed the J&K Protection of Human Rights Act 1997, extinguishing the State Commission. The measured record is in the national Commission's own annual reports, retrieved from its own server. J&K cases registered ran 194 in 2017-18, 218 in 2018-19, 160 in 2019-20, 282 in 2020-21, 465 in 2021-22, 379 in 2022-23 and 995 in 2023-24, with a Ladakh row appearing from 2019-20. The abolition is visible inside the same reports' arithmetic: the column recording J&K cases transferred to State Human Rights Commissions ran 38 in 2017-18 and 51 in 2018-19, fell to 10 in 2019-20 and has been zero in every year since - so complainants in every other State have two bodies and complainants in J&K have one. One column decides the substitution question and it is empty for a different reason: the annual reports carry a 'Defence/Para-Military Custodial Deaths and Rapes' intimation column, and the J&K row reads zero in every year from 2017-18 to 2022-23, against all-India values of 1, 2, 0, 1, 1 and 6 - a column that records intimations received rather than complaints made. What the Commission does not publish is the fraction of J&K complaints whose named respondent is the Army, the Rashtriya Rifles or a central armed police force, and section 19 of its own Act means that for that class it may only seek a report from the Central Government and then drop the matter or recommend: it cannot summon, cannot compel and cannot establish a fact of its own. Section 2(1)(a) defines armed forces to include any other armed forces of the Union, which brings in the central armed police forces.
caseFor: The pre-2019 architecture was a second state-level commission sitting under a national one, and on the hardest cases in the territory it could do nothing at all: the United Nations human rights office recorded in June 2018 that the State Commission did not send a notice to the Indian Army because it had no jurisdiction over forces controlled by the central government operating in Kashmir. A body that cannot notice the principal respondent in the theatre is not an accountability mechanism for that theatre, and its recommendations were non-binding in any event - a limitation the national Commission itself has asked the Central Government to remove for all state commissions. Against that, the reorganisation deleted the proviso that had kept the national Act out of the territory, so for the first time a better-resourced body with a national investigation division and statutory reporting to Parliament has ordinary jurisdiction there; the same schedule extended the central Right to Information Act with its penalty provisions, the National Commission for Women Act, the child rights commissions Act and the Prevention of Corruption Act. And the record shows the national body working the territory: registrations rose from 210 in the last full pre-break year to 982 in 2023-24, monetary relief has been recommended in J&K cases in several years, and the Supreme Court has pressed for a mechanism letting people file from the territory itself. A duplicate and partly ornamental layer was removed and a stronger one extended, and the rise in registrations is what substitution looks like when it works.
caseAgainst: A commission actively examining more than 630 complaints alleging murder, enforced disappearance and rape by security forces was extinguished by a line in a schedule, with no successor named and no arrangement for its files, and its records have sat in a locked room at its former premises ever since. No effort was made to transfer them to the national Commission. The body said to have replaced it cannot investigate the respondents those complaints name: section 19 was not touched by the reorganisation, and for any complaint against the armed forces - a class the Act defines to include any other armed forces of the Union, and so the central armed police forces - the Commission may only seek a report and then drop the matter or recommend. In the one territory where central forces do most of the holding, the substitute is statutorily blind to the principal respondent, and the twenty-four-hour custodial-death intimation duty does not run to those forces either. Nor is the substitution visible in the instruments that would show it. Referrals of J&K cases to a state commission ran at 38 and 51 in the two full years before the abolition and have been zero in every year since. No camp sitting or open hearing was held in the territory in any year for which a report has been published. The one dimension that ever identified armed-forces and paramilitary complaints as such was all-India only, was never crossed with the state dimension, and was discontinued after the 2021-22 report. And the arithmetic that would settle whether any of this amounts to substitution has never been published, because nobody publishes what fraction of J&K complaints concern forces the national Commission may not investigate.
differentFactsNote: Flagged false and noted, because the two cases look as though they cross a category boundary - a rising complaint count against a statutory bar - and they do not. Precondition (b) holds: granting the case for its strongest fact in full, that the State Commission had no jurisdiction over centrally controlled forces, leaves the case against untouched, because 630 complaints still abated and section 19 still bars the national Commission; and granting the case against in full leaves the extension of the national Act intact. But criterion (c) fails, and it fails for the ordinary reason the criterion names. The common measure exists in principle: it is the fraction of J&K complaints registered with the national Commission whose named respondent is the Army, the Rashtriya Rifles or a central armed police force. The Commission assigns an incident code to every case and records the state of origin of every case, and it prints both facts separately in the same document - a body that can print two columns can produce their intersection. The comparison is unbuilt, not unbuildable, and an unbuilt comparison fails (c) expressly. That the one number which would decide the argument is the one nobody has printed is the finding, and it is a gap in the instrument rather than a property of the argument.

title: Seven commissions wound up by seven consecutive orders on one day, and the word pending appears in none of them
summary: On 23 October 2019 the General Administration Department of Jammu and Kashmir issued seven government orders, numbered 1143 to 1149 consecutively, under one file number and one signature, winding up seven state commissions with effect from the appointed day: human rights, information, consumer disputes, electricity regulation, persons with disabilities, protection of women and child rights, and accountability. Each order disposes of the Commissioner, the staff, the vehicles, the building and the furniture, and directs the records to an administrative department for record. None of them mentions a pending case.
whatHappened: The seven orders were retrieved individually from the issuing department's own order server and read. The identifiers on either side of the run are unrelated business - compassionate appointments, the Darbar Move, an expenditure restriction - and nothing readable sits above the run, so the seven were issued as one act of administration. The Human Rights Commission order recites that consequent upon the repeal of the 1997 Act by the Reorganisation Act, sanction is accorded to the winding up with effect from 31 October 2019, the appointed date. The Information Commission order is in the same form and its clause (vi) sends all records pertaining to the Commission to the General Administration Department for record. The word 'pending' does not appear in either. That is now established across two independently retrieved orders, which makes it a pattern rather than an oversight in one document. The consequence for the information forum is measurable at both ends and is unusually clean for this phase. The State Information Commission ceased on 31 October 2019; the Central Information Commission's own published decision index returns zero decisions against any Jammu and Kashmir public authority for any order date up to 14 May 2020, and its earliest is 15 May 2020. So for 197 days no forum decided a second appeal from Jammu and Kashmir, and both endpoints come from the successor body's own index. The Commission's last published pendency figure dates from 31 March 2014, five years stale at abolition, so it cannot be used to size what abated. Its web presence died with it: the host returned HTTP 200 on 8 October 2019 and 404 from 7 November 2019, and does not resolve at all now. The one J&K-specific figure anyone has put on the record since is a Secretary's letter to the Chief Secretary in January 2026 giving roughly 600 pending second appeals, which a newspaper obtained. The successor publishes its caseload as three national totals only, with no state or Union Territory breakdown, in an annual report currently sixteen months behind and, in its most recent edition, an image-only scan with no text layer.
caseFor: Repealing the enabling statute of a body and then formally winding the body up is the ordinary administrative consequence of a legislative act, not a separate decision, and an order that disposes of vehicles, buildings and staff is doing exactly what a winding-up order is for. Central successors existed and were extended by the same schedule: the central Right to Information Act with its penalty provisions replaced the State Act, and the Central Information Commission accepted the transfer of pending matters with due seniority on a plan settled in Delhi eight days before the winding-up order was signed. The records were not destroyed - the order sends them to a named department, which is a custodian on the face of the instrument - and the successor commission did begin deciding J&K appeals within seven months. Seven consecutive order numbers on one day is what a single administrative event looks like when it is executed tidily rather than what a hidden decision looks like.
caseAgainst: Seven forums before which a citizen could bring a grievance against the state were closed by seven sheets of paper signed on one day by one Secretary, and not one of them says what becomes of a case that was live. The orders dispose of furniture and electronic gadgets by name and consign the caseload to silence, sending 'all records pertaining to the Commission' to an administrative department 'for record' - a phrase for storage, not for adjudication. The plan for the pending cases lived in a letter from Delhi that no public repository holds. And the gap is measurable: 197 days in which no forum anywhere decided a second appeal from Jammu and Kashmir, established from the successor's own published index at both ends. The successor then publishes nothing that would let anyone see the territory's caseload at all - three national totals, no state breakdown, a report sixteen months late and latterly unreadable by machine - so the only J&K number on the record since is one that leaked from a letter. The last published pendency figure for the abolished Commission is from 2014, so nobody can even say how many appeals were extinguished.
assessmentNote: Filed no-objective because no objective was stated at announcement against which any of the seven orders could be scored. The orders recite a repeal and accord sanction to a winding-up; they claim nothing and promise nothing, which is precisely the finding. The value asserts nothing about the quality of what is established: all seven orders were retrieved from the issuing department's own server, and both endpoints of the 197-day gap come from the successor commission's own published index.
